## What this document is for

 Two different things are collected here, and the difference is the whole point of the "7 ready-now / 3 behind blockers" split:

-  **Phases 1–7** are things Claude can do **right now**, start to finish, with no professional appointment, no licence, and no purchase standing in the way.

-  Phases 8–10 are not new versions of the CTA/licence/surveyor prep already done. That prep exists and is real, and Phase 51 (31 Aug 2026) went further: the ten adviser-gated engine defects are no longer inert patches waiting outside the source — all ten are BUILT INTO the live engine behind named switches in LS_CTA, both readings implemented and tested, every switch defaulting to current behaviour. Six licence-gated data connections already have their mechanisms built with empty, clearly-labelled stubs; four surveyor-facing documents already have straw men waiting for a correction pass. Phases 8–10 go one layer deeper than that.


## The goal behind both

 Every phase below serves one aim: **make each part of the business as automated and as fully specified as possible before it is handed to an accountant, a surveyor or a developer.** Phase 7 exists specifically to package that handover.

## Before touching anything

 This board runs a **multi-machine protocol**. The board is the source of truth for status, not this doc.

1.  Open the item on Monday by its ID/URL.

2.  Check it isn't already claimed — look at **Status** and **"Claimed by (machine)."**

3.  Set **Status = "Working on it"** and fill **"Claimed by (machine)"** with this machine's name.

4.  Do the work, then set Status to whatever's correct (Done / Awaiting CTA review / Blocked) and clear the claim.

 This doc is a **priority order**, not a lock. Phases don't need to run in strict sequence, but within Phases 8–10, do not start until the corresponding "what already exists" section has been read.

## A note on environment

 Every phase below produces a **document** — a spec, a policy, a comparison note, a template — never application code. If you are picking this up in a session with codebase access, the specs in Phases 5, 8 and 9 are written so a developer session can implement directly from them. If you have no codebase access, every phase is still fully completable: read the referenced board items and attached files, write the deliverable, attach it, comment, and move on.

---

## Standing rules — apply in every phase

1.  **Claim before you touch.** Set Status = "Working on it" and fill Claimed by (machine) before starting an item. Clear the claim when you finish or abandon.

2.  **Claude drafts, a named human approves.** Never mark a policy, an assessment or a tax position as final.

3.  **No rate may be stated that is not in Rulebook I.** Scottish income tax rates are not yet in Rulebook I — no Scottish figure may be quoted anywhere until the Addendum (12889350666) is reviewed.

4.  **"Refund" language belongs only to routes W1 and W4.** On W2 there is no refund, only reduced tax over time.

5.  **Never cite a case, a statute or a piece of guidance you have not actually read.**

6.  **A reasoned negative is a deliverable, not a failure.** See item 12804151034.

7.  **No date is invented.** Where a plan needs a date, say what it depends on instead.

8.  **Verify every tax rate by search before use.** Never assert from memory.

9.  **Every phase is a copy-paste prompt, and every phase deletes ****itsel****f****.** Each phase section below is a large-title heading, a bold Model line, and one fenced block holding the entire self-contained prompt — copy the block verbatim into a fresh session, nothing else needed. Every such prompt carries its own claim-first instruction, its own escalation rules, and its own instruction to remove itself. On completion the phase deletes its own heading, Model line and block from this document, and records what it delivered as a row in the "what's confirmed complete" table. That is how this doc stays a to-do list rather than a log. The sweep phase is the sole exception: it renumbers forward instead of deleting, so the convention itself survives.


10.  **Nothing a phase cannot resolve may be left as prose. Prose is not a task.** Before a phase closes it takes one of three actions on anything it could not finish. Blocked on a decision only Lakhbir, the CTA, the DPO or a surveyor can make — add a numbered question to QUESTIONS TO BE ANSWERED (item 12919337890) with a one-line "why it matters" and a recommendation, or "none, this needs your judgement" where there honestly is none. A concrete gap with no board item — create the item, in the right group, with Owner type set, named so it is actionable without that conversation. Work too large for an item, needing its own drafting session — write it into this document as a new phase in the format at rule 9, numbered after the highest existing phase, with the sweep kept last. An item must never be marked Done while work it could not finish exists only as a sentence in a document.


11.  **Confirm every write by reading it back, and keep the document title in step with the document.** A mutation's success response is not proof the write landed: an item rename over **255 characters** returns success and silently leaves the old name (item 12929302538), while `create_item` refuses the same string with an explicit error — so the platform enforces the rule on one path and not the other. After any rename, status change or doc edit that records an outcome, read it back in a separate query. Where the outcome will not fit in 255 characters, put it in an **item update**, which has no such limit, and keep the name short. And when a phase reissues a document at a new version, rename **both** the board item and the document itself — Phase 46 found the build plan's content at v14 under a title still reading v13, and the decision queue at v7.0 under a title reading v6.9. Nothing had failed; the convention simply only ever renamed the item, and to a reader the effect is identical to a silent failure.

12.  **Test a "this cannot be done" before you inherit it.** Four times in five sweeps a blocker recorded on this board has turned out to be false: a corrupted status label "not fixable via API" (one call fixed it), a failing test that "needs a taxonomy judgement, not a test edit" (one pass fixed it), a document-writing API "down platform-wide" (it worked first time), and "ico.org.uk returns 403 so ICO guidance cannot be read" (it blocks one fetch method; a browser reads the site normally). Each was true of the exact thing tried, and each was then copied forward by every phase that read it. **A blocker is only established once it has been retried by a different method.** A wrong "only a human can do this" costs more than the bug it describes, because it parks work in somebody's queue that was never theirs.

|  **44 — Where the upload control actually sits, and the retention option that had no producer** |  Opus 5 |  Both items closed; `phase3` **262 → 287 tests, 0 fail**; harness unchanged at **238 pass / 0 fail / 14 xfail**. **(A) 12928214881 — the boundary.** Q40 is unanswered, so the module is built against the **quarantine-prefix** model as a **fail-closed default**, and says so in a field (`INGESTION_BOUNDARY.is_a_decision = false`) rather than in a paragraph. New in `ledgerstone-client-doc-ingestion.ts` sections 1A–1C: `assertQuarantineKey` (a pre-signed URL for a key outside the quarantine prefix is refused — one string compare on which the whole model rests), `quarantineDischargeDueAt`, `sweepQuarantine`, `recordQuarantineDischarge` and `assertQuarantineDischarged`, with **two refusals that are different in kind** — `E_DURABLE_WRITE_BEFORE_STRIP` (promotion before, or without, the strip: the ordering _is_ the control, and a quarantine step done in the wrong order is direct-to-durable with an extra copy) and `E_QUARANTINE_UNDISCHARGED` (past the 60-minute TTL and still held: the quiet failure, where quarantine silently becomes a second durable store). `RECEIPT_CONTRACT` rewritten from 9 steps to 12 and now **names the quarantine write as a real write** and its deletion as a step. **The overstatements are corrected, not the control weakened:** `applyReceiptPolicy`'s doc comment, `ReceiptResult.removed`, contract steps 3–4 and the `E_TRANSPARENCY_NO_BASIS_ROLE` message all now say it filters extracted text. `BOUNDARY_POSITION` records, for all three models, that **only server-mediated upload ever made Phase 41's sentence true**. **(B) 12928215019 — the option with no producer.** `RETAIN_REDACTED_DELETE_ORIGINAL` **withdrawn**, not merely flagged: gone from `RawFileRetentionRule`, refused at runtime by `assertRetentionRuleImplementable` (settings come from config; a union type is not a guard), and `recordDeletion` now refuses `redacted_copy_retained: true` outright — nothing can produce one, so the flag was a protection asserted into existence. Withdrawal chosen over building because the quarantine step makes a producer **buildable but not built**, and shipping the guarantee ahead of the mechanism is the defect itself; `REDACTION_PRODUCER_CONTRACT` states the six things a real producer must do (destroy the text, handle the raster path, reach every copy the format keeps, refuse rather than guess, **verify by re-extracting**, run inside the quarantine window) so reinstatement is a build against a spec. **(C) Condition D4 re-checked and downgraded to PARTLY MET** (`CONDITION_D4_STATUS`) — met for the extracted text, not met for the file. **The consequence nobody had drawn:** D4 is a lawful-basis condition, so `RETAIN_FOR_DEFENCE_PERIOD` cannot apply to a document whose strip removed `NO_LAWFUL_BASIS` content — such a record now falls back to the extraction clock automatically. Fail-closed for a retention rule means **delete sooner**, and it does. The flag is **derived** from the receipt by `rawFileRecordFromReceipt`, never caller-asserted. **Tests:** 15 boundary (B1–B15) plus 10 withdrawal and constraint (X1–X10). **B15 is unusual on purpose** — it reads the module's own source and fails if the overstated wording is ever _asserted_ again, masking double-quoted spans so the corrections may still quote it. Three phases in a row made this mistake in prose, and prose has no type system. **Queue:** v6.9 — **Q44** (do you accept that planning documents lose the long clock) and **Q45** (fund the redaction producer?); **Q34 annotated to two answers**, **Q41 marked ACTIONED**, **Q40 annotated as built-to-by-default and no longer blocking**. |

### The two things the sweep found, and they are the same shape as Phase 40's

 **Both are new, both are on the board, and both were written up as Phase 44.** Phase 44 ran on 30 August 2026 and closed both — see its row in the completion table above. Kept here as the record of what the sweep found, not as open work.

1.  **Item 12928214881 — the receipt strip runs after the file is already stored.** `applyReceiptPolicy` says it removes segments "on receipt, before the first write" and "drops them out of _the document_". But `STORAGE_POSITION` records the architecture of record as **AWS S3 with pre-signed URLs**, which means the browser writes the file straight to durable storage and Ledgerstone's code never holds it first. The strip filters the **extracted text**; the original keeps everything, for the whole retention period, and that file is where Phase 40 §5.4 establishes the entire third-party personal data holding lives. **Condition D4, stated as absolute, is not.** Phase 40 found the control one boundary downstream of the duty; Phase 41 moved it to "receipt"; the sweep found the door had moved again.

2.  **Item 12928215019 — one of Q34's three answers cannot be performed.** `RETAIN_REDACTED_DELETE_ORIGINAL` promises "a copy with the receipt strip applied". **Nothing anywhere produces a redacted file** — there is no PDF or image redaction in the codebase, `applyReceiptPolicy` returns text segments, `redacted_copy_retained` is a boolean a caller asserts, and `deletionDueAt` treats the option as identical to plain deletion. It is the option Phase 40 §7.7 measure 2 recommends, and it is offered to Lakhbir and the DPO inside Q34 as a live choice. **A decision is being put to a human with an option that does not work**, and neither Q34 nor the module says so. Q41 annotates it.

### The one thing this sweep found

 **There were six cross-references, not five, and the sixth was the one that mattered most.** Phase 43 read both documents, found five where Phase 31 §4.2 had named three, corrected all five, and recorded the total as five. Reading the Business Continuity Plan end to end found a sixth: **§8 "Invocation", "What they do first", point (4)** — _"whether personal data may be involved, and if so, start the privacy-policy breach process in parallel, not after."_

 This is variant (i) of the pattern in its purest form. Phase 43's correction was complete on its own terms — it swept the scope sections, the scenario steps and the escalation table — and §8 is none of those. It is the **invocation** section: the half-page somebody actually reads at the moment they declare an incident, which is precisely the moment the pointer has to be right. **Corrected on 30 August 2026.** The plan has also been given a version number (1.1), a date pair and an amendment record, none of which it had despite having been amended twice without a reader being able to tell.

### The thing this sweep found, and it is the same shape as the thing Phase 45 found

 **The A5 miss.** Phase 43 reported adding two consequentials Phase 35 had not named: **A5** and A9. A9 landed in the body text. **A5 did not.** Its correction existed only as a row in the A1A.2 table — the scope table near the top of the carve-out — while A5 itself, headed **"Who investigates"**, still read exactly as v1.0: every complaint investigated by Lakhbir in the first instance, and a complaint about Lakhbir referred to the firm's solicitor. Both are wrong for a s.164A data protection complaint, which is the DPO's to classify, investigate, decide and notify, countersigned but not instructable, with a statutory independent route rather than the firm's solicitor.

 **Why it survived a verification pass that was specifically looking for this.** Part A's own version line reads "consequential corrections at **A2, A4, A8 and A9**". Phase 45 checked those four, found all four present, and wrote "Confirmed". The board item's name says **A5 and A9**. The document under-reported itself by one section, and the verification took the document's word for its own scope. _This is why a count must be re-derived from the thing counted, not from any list the artefact offers about itself — for the third sweep running._

 **Why A5 is the expensive one to miss.** It is the section titled "Who investigates" — what a person opens when a complaint has arrived and they need to know what to do. The same shape as Phase 45's BCP §8: a correction complete on its own terms and absent from the one section somebody reads under pressure. The fix also states something A1A.2's row assumed and never said — that the DPO route is **not yet operative** because the instrument of appointment is unsigned (Q43) — without which A5 would have offered a route that cannot currently be performed.

### The blocker that was false, and it is the fourth in five sweeps

 **"ico.org.uk returns HTTP 403 to automated requests, so ICO guidance could not be read."** Recorded in five documents — Item 5, the Retention Procedure, the pre-solicitor research note, the DPO instrument (§2.3 and §12) and governance §A1A.3 — and load-bearing in each: it is the stated reason a `[VERIFY]` sits open on an unsigned instrument, the reason §A1A.3 cites no ICO guidance at all, and part of why item 12927942615 was parked on Lakhbir.

 **It is a statement about one fetch method.** WebFetch is refused with 403; the in-app browser loads the site normally. Both were run side by side on two ICO URLs. Two pages were then read, and each closed something open:

-  **The DPO guidance confirms §2.3 in terms** — "If you decide to voluntarily appoint a DPO you should be aware that the same requirements of the position and tasks apply had the appointment been mandatory", with the same point repeated as a checklist commitment. The `[VERIFY]` is closed on the instrument and review trigger §9.2(5) is discharged.

-  **The breach-reporting page answers most of item 12927942615** — route, the five question groups, and the operational fact that matters most: **the form cannot be saved and resumed**. That item is retagged Lakhbir → Claude. New item **12929498804** lists the five documents still carrying the false claim.

 After Phase 30's corrupted status label, Phase 42's "needs a taxonomy judgement" and Phase 45's "the document API is down platform-wide", **four of the last five sweeps have disproved a blocker.** Each claim was true of the exact thing tried; none was ever retried a second way. That is now standing rule 12.

### Smaller things the sweep did directly

-  **The Developer Brief's §11 and §12.** §11 listed "signed URLs" among settled security controls with no flag — and §11 is where a developer scopes and prices. §12, _Open decisions to confirm_, listed the booking vendor and the e-signature vendor but **not** the upload boundary, the only decision on it that changes where a statutory duty attaches. Both fixed. A stale "a short DPIA is recommended" corrected — one exists at v1.1 with two High residual risks. And a rendering fault fixed: Phase 44 had inserted its flag **inside** the §3 technology-stack table, splitting it so the second half rendered without headers.

-  **The Rules-Defect plan was amended and never versioned.** Phase 45 gave the BCP a version, a date pair and an amendment record for exactly this reason — and did it only for the BCP, leaving the second document in the same Phase 43 correction reading "v1.0, 29 August" after being changed. Now **v1.1** with an amendment record, and the outstanding reciprocal cross-reference (BCP §10, conditional on both being approved) written down so it is not chased as a defect.

-  **Both index documents had stale titles.** This plan's content was at v14 under a title reading v13; the decision queue's content was at v7.0 under a title reading v6.9. Nothing failed — the convention only ever renamed the board item. Standing rule 11 now covers it.

-  **Four items in group Z at "Awaiting CTA review"** moved to 06 · Reports & Deliverables and read back (12929275226 closed). No status changed; the contradiction was on the face of the board.

-  **Two self-reported counts re-derived and found wrong.** Item 12927607388 still says **28** blank subitems under Done parents in Z; the figure has been **23 across 8 parents** since Phase 33 ticked five. The decision queue's header said "47 questions" when 47 numbers had been issued and Q13 is retired — 46 live, now 47 with Q48. Both corrected on the record.

-  **Decision queue reissued at v7.1** with **Q48** (whether to start a live ICO breach report purely to see the form — recommendation: no).

### What the sweep looked for and did NOT find, recorded so the next one does not re-derive it

-  **The unperformable-option test comes back clean across Q34, Q35, Q40, Q41 and Q46.** Phase 45 cleared Q34's two survivors and Q35's two options; this pass adds Q46 and confirms the earlier result. No option currently in front of Lakhbir is one the system could not perform once the storage adapter exists.

-  **No historical rename shows evidence of silent truncation.** All 310 item names measured; eleven are ≥250 characters, four are exactly 255, and each of those four was read in full and ends on a complete, deliberately-fitted clause. **This test is weak by construction and should not be repeated as though it were strong** — a failed rename leaves the _old_ name, which looks like any other name, so "no anomalies" is not "no failures". The preventive rule (standing rule 11) is worth more than the search.

-  **`03-app/phase3`**** and ****`03-app/phase9`**** are symlinks into ****`04-phase-work/`****, not copies.** They appear in a directory listing exactly as a divergent fork would. They are not one, and there is no second copy of the phase3 code anywhere in the store.

-  **The two Z parents carrying the most blank subitems are correctly blank.** 12818313893 (11 of 13) and 12818978746 (10 of 10) hold **catalogue rows** — one per data source, one per document type — not tasks. Any future count of "blank subitems under Done parents" must exclude them, or it returns 10 parents / 44 subitems instead of the true 8 / 23.

### The thing this sweep found, and it is the same shape as the last two

 **Phase 46 disproved a blocker and then corrected one of the six places it sat.** The "ico.org.uk returns 403, guidance cannot be read" claim was recorded in Item 5 (twice), the Retention Procedure (twice), the pre-solicitor research note (twice), the DPO instrument (§2.3 and §12) and governance §A1A.3. Phase 46 fixed **§2.3 alone** and created item 12929498804 listing the rest.

 **The sharpest consequence was inside a single document.** For a day, the DPO instrument's **§2.3** said the ICO guidance had been read and confirmed the reading, while **§12 — the section headed "what could not be verified" — said it could not be read at all.** A reader going to §12 to find out what was unverified would have been told to distrust a conclusion the same document had already closed. That is Phase 45's BCP §8 and Phase 46's A5 again: _the correction lands everywhere except the place somebody checks._

 **All six are now corrected, and in each case the guidance was read rather than the sentence deleted.** That is the part that mattered:

-  **Item 5 §2.7's ****`[VERIFY]`**** is closed.** The ICO's "Legitimate interests" page (updated 23 March 2026) gives the three-part test **word for word** — purpose, necessity, balancing — plus the requirements that it precede processing, be documented as an LIA, and fail on necessity where a less intrusive route exists. Also recorded so it is not re-opened: the ICO treats _recognised legitimate interest_ (Art 6(1)(ea), Annex 1) as a **separate basis**, and no Annex 1 purpose reaches register lookups — Art 6(1)(f) stands. **Item 5 → v1.2.**

-  **The research note's §A3 caveat is withdrawn.** "Personal data breaches: a guide": _"a security incident that has affected the confidentiality, integrity or availability of personal data"_. Every limb is a security event. This **strengthens** A3 and finding S3. **→ v1.1.**

-  **Retention Procedure Appendix A** — same DPO flag Phase 46 closed elsewhere, closed here. **→ v1.1.**

-  **DPO instrument §12 and §9.2(5)** — §9.2(5) marked _discharged, fired and did not bite_, deliberately not deleted because the ICO page carries a DUAA review notice. **→ v1.1**, which also records Phase 46's §2.3 edit; Phase 46 had not versioned it.

-  **Governance §A1A.3** — corrected. **→ v1.1.**

 **The Retention Procedure §6 carried an open ****`[VERIFY]`**** that another document had explicitly closed two days earlier.** §6 asked the DPO to confirm the onward complaint route now Article 77 is omitted. **Section 5 of the Rights-Request Register and s.164A Complaints Pack (item 12927908435) is headed **_**"THE ONWARD ROUTE — THE [VERIFY] AT RETENTION PROCEDURE 6, CLOSED"**_ and works it out in full from the legislation: Art 77 omitted, DPA 2018 s.165(1) omitted, and **s.165(2) widened by the insertion of "the UK GDPR or"** — all on 19 June 2026, same section, same commencement instrument. The right moved out of the Regulation into the Act. §6 is now closed with that answer and points at §5.7 of the pack for the public-page wording. **Phase 41 found the retention answer in the Developer Brief; this is the same pattern, and the closing document even named the section it was closing.**

### A count three sweeps got wrong, where the error was hiding the only real risk

 `03-app/` was recorded as holding **"seven byte-identical duplicates"**, md5-verified on three separate passes, each concluding "a filing question, not a correctness risk". `stat` shows what md5 cannot: **six of the seven are hard links** — link count 2, **same inode** under both paths. One file, two names. Zero extra disk, and they **cannot** diverge. **`Ledgerstone-Fixture-Taxonomy-v1.csv`**** is the exception** — distinct inodes, a genuine second copy, identical today with nothing keeping it so, and the most-edited artefact of the seven.

 **So a check re-run on seven files every sweep was reassuring the one that could fail with the six that could not.** `README-file-index.md` corrected; item 12927609775 is now a one-file decision. **The general form is worth carrying: a control that re-verifies N things every pass, most of which cannot fail, is not a control.**

 **The finding that changed a method rather than a number.** RD-01 counted fire-detection points by floor area. On a real 268 m² dental fit-out that gives **2.4–4.8 points**; a room-by-room count gives **15–19**. That is not a coefficient that needs tuning — it is answering a different question, because **detection follows compartmentation, not floor area**: a 14 m² surgery needs its own detector whether the building is 268 m² or 2,680. The room-driven method is now primary and area-density is demoted to a **labelled sanity floor** that the type system will not let anyone emit as a result (`resolution_path` has no `area_density` value). The same defect shape was found and fixed in RD-13, and a new sanity-floor check now flags a room count that falls _below_ the area floor as an incomplete room schedule rather than silently replacing it.

 **Two things were deliberately built without being chosen.** Depreciation now has both methods behind one switch — per element (LEG-E5) and whole building (LEG-E5b) — defaulting to `none`, which is today's behaviour exactly. The one back-compatibility rule runs **one way only**: E5's gate on with no method stated still resolves to per-element, but E5b's gate on never self-selects, and both gates on resolves to `none` because that is the configuration where a genuine choice exists. Same discipline as Phase 51.

 **The calibration item stays blocked, and correctly so — but its instrument is now built.** No document can produce calibration data; that finding from 28 August stands. What was wrong was the conclusion that therefore nothing could be built. Three parts of the instrument **cannot be retrofitted**: the blank-field control (a control needs an unanchored arm, and every job run before it starts is already anchored), the acceptance-versus-never-looked distinction (it has to be captured at the moment, not inferred), and which of the two meanings of "adoption" is being measured (they produce an identical number and it is not recoverable afterwards which one it was). All three are now built and stamped. Every reading says `INSUFFICIENT_DATA`, which is the correct output of a correctly built instrument with nothing in it.

 **The report template's "63% resolved" was not missing analysis.** It was 36 cells where a professional judgement had been correctly identified and then left as `*[blank]*` — indistinguishable, to a reader, from not having thought about it. Every one now carries the question it was standing in for, 34 numbered questions collected at §24 with a five-question priority set. **No pre-filled judgement figure was added anywhere**; the v1 discipline is unchanged.

 **On the price books.** The three Spon's PDFs were used as an internal sanity check only and **no rate, band or figure was transcribed anywhere**. Outcomes recorded in `price-book-sanity-check-outcomes-v1.md`; the extracted text was deleted. The useful finding is commercial, not technical: the M&E book covers hospitals and GP surgeries and contains **nothing at all for dental practices or care homes** — the two sectors the pilot leads with. In those two, a surveyor is not a second opinion on our figure, they are the only opinion available, and the engagement should be scoped and priced as that.

 **Status set to "Waiting on someone else", not "Awaiting CTA review".** The phase brief said "Awaiting review"; the board has no such label, and the only existing near-match is CTA-specific and would route six surveyor items to the wrong professional. Flagged rather than mislabelled — if a `Surveyor review` label is wanted, it needs adding to the Status column.

 **The handler is the substantive change, and the reason it mattered.** `RECEIPT_CONTRACT` had stated a twelve-step call order since 30 August and **nothing had ever called it**. Eighty-two tests passed against a module with no consumer — which proves the design is coherent and proves nothing about whether one client document is protected. Every control on client documents was dormant in the exact sense that no code path reached it. Two guarantees are now enforced: **nothing is promoted to durable storage before the strip has run** (three independent enforcements, because the failure is silent), and **the quarantine object is deleted with the deletion recorded, on the failure path as well as the success path**. Where the store's delete itself fails the job does **not** report success and the object is left undischarged, so the scheduled sweep raises it within the TTL — a handler that swallowed a failed delete would be worse than no handler, because it would look like one.

 **It is written against ports, not against a store, and that is the WordPress answer.** `ObjectStore` and `AuditSink` are five methods and one method. Q40, Q51 and Q52 all change the adapter and none changes the design.

 **THE ESCALATION, and it is the reason §3.0 was written before anything else.** WordPress has no object store. `wp-content/uploads/` sits inside the webroot and is served **with no authorisation check at all**. Three controls the data protection work depends on were assessed against it and **not designed around**: storage separation (**C1**), evidenced deletion (**C2** — a file deleted from disk and alive in a host's nightly snapshot has not been deleted, and the deletion record would say it had), and the immutable audit log (**C3** — a log every WordPress Administrator can edit, including the record of their own actions, is not an audit log). Two are meetable only by not using WordPress's own machinery; the third is not meetable inside WordPress at all. They are now **Q51, Q52 and Q53** in the decision queue, in plain English, for Lakhbir and the DPO, plus **Q54** — whether WordPress replaces the Node back end or sits beside it, which is two different quotes and must be answered before anybody prices this. **Only the client-document upload page waits on any of them. The rest of the build proceeds.**

 **Two questions had fallen out of the decision queue.** The v8.0 plain-English rewrite dropped **Q40** and **Q46** — the two that decide where a statutory duty attaches to client documents, so the last two that should have gone. Both are restored in Part 5 of v8.2. Q46 is now moot: the handler is built.

 **One client-facing defect found and fixed while verifying deliverable 1.** The s.187A closed-window handoff put `board item 12921346993` into `action`, which renders **to the client** in the "Why a specialist needs to look" panel; five sector flags carried two more board ids. One string was doing two jobs for two audiences. The internal half now lives in a `ref` field and in source comments, and **Suite M fails if any client-facing string carries a board item number again**. The harness assertion that had locked the old behaviour in was corrected rather than deleted, and its mirror added.

 **One finding recorded rather than fixed, because it is not a defect.** `extract()` and `captureHumanRead()` both iterate the SPEC's field list, so a field a model invents — a person's name included — is dropped before claims exist. `assertClaimsWritable` at step 10 is therefore **not** the barrier between a model and an unauthorised name; the spec is, and the name control is the second of two. What step 10 actually guards is **drift**: a DOC_SPEC growing a field the register has not catalogued. Test N1b is the only place that refusal is currently reachable, and it is reachable only by constructing it.

With Lakhbir as both controller and deputy **that control collapses and the countersignature adds nothing, because it is the same signature.** Claude's own recommendation at breach-procedure §7.1 Q23 was that the deputy could not be Lakhbir alone, for exactly that reason; **the recommendation was put, considered and declined, and that is written down rather than dropped.** It is defensible at this size — the realistic alternative was no weekend route at all — and §6.7 and ADDENDUM 3 both say what would remove it: any second person with no commercial interest in the engagement could countersign, the countersignature is a review rather than a decision, and it can be given after the notification has gone.

It holds out of hours even after the account exists, because the contactability undertaking Q23 offered as the alternative was not taken and nothing obliges the DPO to be reachable at a weekend.

# PHASE 59 — DONE, 1 September 2026 (L.Dhillon-WIN11). Prompt deleted.

 **Delivered.** A two-route identity standard for a rights request, written into **Retention and Rights-Request Operating Procedure v1.3** (item 12818099921, Document 2 — doc 18428630726), with a matching build specification in the **Developer Brief at v3.2, new §5.2a**, and the note the phase was asked to leave on item 12878920167.

 **The answer was adopted in full and it covered one of the two populations.** Lakhbir's standard — _name, affiliation with the organisation, approval from the company owner or director to speak on the company's behalf, captured on the back end system_ — is **Route A**, unchanged, at 5.5.2. It is a good test for a client company's director or practice manager. **It cannot be passed by the population the control was written for:** a private individual named in a lease or a property enquiry reply a client uploaded has no company, no affiliation with us and no director who could approve them. Applying it to them refuses every request they could ever make, which is a breach of Article 12(2) rather than a strict standard. **So Route B was written rather than the gap inherited** — which is what the phase brief asked for, and it is recorded on the board item in those words.

 **Route B's shape, and it is the one the complaints pack had already recommended at Q26 rather than a new invention.** Public matching data is enough to **FIND** the record and is not enough to **RELEASE** it — for an E1 person with significant control the matching data is a name plus a birth month and year **that Companies House publishes**, so a stranger who passes it has proved only that they can use a search box (breach register W7). Release takes one corroborating fact only that person would hold — the property or instruction, a reference from us, who supplied the document, the nature or date of the dealing, or a reply to a one-time code sent to an address already on the record — **or** a narrower disclosure giving everything Article 15(1) requires except the non-public content. **What does not count is enumerated too**, because leaving it implicit is how a purchasable fact gets recorded as a control: name, birth month and year, nationality, company number, registered office, officer appointments, PSC status, and the HMLR title number and proprietor name.

 **Three consequences of Route A that do not change it**, at 5.5.2. (1) **It is an authority test, not an identity test** — "approval from a director" answers _may this person speak for the company_, not _is this person who they say_; the identity half comes from an account we issued, and where the representative has no account Route A has no identity half at all and Route B's check is applied to them too. (2) **The grantor must be someone we can already place** — on the instruction, or an officer on the Companies House record we already hold; an approval from a name that appears nowhere is a second unverified stranger, and `grantor_placement: NEITHER` exists so the record can say so rather than swallow it. (3) **Company authority is not a third individual's mandate** — Article 15(4), raised as **Q67**.

 **The point that makes the recording load-bearing, and it cuts the other way from the obvious one.** Article 12A(2)(b) restarts the whole month from the day identity information is received, so an identity request **gains time** — one made on day 2 and answered on day 19 hands back all nineteen days. The advantage is real and legitimate, and it is exactly what makes an _unjustified_ identity request profitable. That is why `identity_standard_applied` is mandatory, why 5.5.4 requires the request early and once, and why the developer brief asks for a dashboard warning at seven days.

 **Corpus consistency — occurrences counted, not documents.** Four other places carried the old position and all four were corrected in the same pass: the **complaints pack** (12927908435) Addendum 1 moves readiness **C8** from "NOT DECIDED" to PART-DECIDED; the **response letters pack** (12927850552) Addendum 1 fills the slot **§3.5 had explicitly reserved for this answer** — and records that §3.5's conservative rule was **confirmed rather than replaced**, which is worth stating about a section that predicted its own replacement; **DECISIONS → v14.0**, new Part 13; and the Desktop Blockers map, whose "a second route is needed" now reads as built.

 **Law read first-hand on legislation.gov.uk, 1 September 2026**, rather than carried from the earlier packs: **Article 11(1)–(2)** — which is what makes "we cannot tell which record is yours" a lawful answer rather than a fudge — **Article 12(1)–(6)** including 12(2)'s cross-reference to 11(2), and **Article 15(1A), 15(3) and 15(4)**. No ICO guidance cited.

 **Status, and the honest part.** Route A is decided and needs no approval. **Route B is drafted and NOT approved** — C8 and the open limb of Q26, closing when the DPO signs 5.5.3 — and is **deliberately the operating rule in the meantime**, because the alternative is applying Route A to a private individual, which is a certain breach rather than an unapproved control. **And "captured on the back end system" names a destination, not a running control:** the back end does not exist, none of §5.2a is built, and until it is, both routes are recorded by hand.

 **Escalated rather than guessed — Q67 and Q68**, both with drafted answers needing confirmation rather than decision, both with the DPO. Nothing new waits on Lakhbir.

 **The finding that matters most, and it runs the opposite way to how the reversal was framed.** The old design left the Article 14 duty **unmet** for every person whose address was printed on the document — on the Article 14 Assessment's own analysis, one letter to an address in front of the reader is not a disproportionate effort, it is an argument that fails. **You cannot send that letter to somebody whose name you did not keep.** Holding an identity is what makes the duty performable, and it removes reliance on Article 11(2), which the same document thought would probably fail. **The reversal closed a live non-compliance. That belongs in the record as a benefit of the decision, not a consolation for it.**

 **Escalated rather than resolved — Q69, Q70, Q71** (DECISIONS Part 14). **Q69 is the Article 36 one**, on its own board item 12949133781: not engaged today, because R10 is high pending a question nobody has asked rather than high after mitigation failed — **but if the host says the backup cannot exclude the folder and the business proceeds anyway, that is prior consultation, and the Commissioner has up to fourteen weeks.**

 **The one thing that can stop a build:** B1, item **12949133180**. One email to the host. Nothing about client uploads should be built before it is answered in writing.

 **A mistake this phase made, recorded because it is the fourth time on this board.** The first draft of the dashboard specification restated Phase 41's "the strip runs before the first write". **Phase 44 had already killed that**, and test B15 exists to refuse the wording. It was caught by running the suite. **Correcting it produced the two best findings in the phase** — a sixth store (S0, the quarantine object), and the widening of B1 to cover it, which is the more urgent half because that object holds the file unredacted including content there is no lawful basis to hold at all. **Read the architecture where it is written down as data, next to the control — not from the phase document that describes it.**

 **Test evidence:** `ledgerstone-client-doc-ingestion.test.ts` **82 pass, 0 fail**; `ledgerstone-name-exclusion.test.ts` **22 pass, 0 fail**; node v24.16.0, run after the edits. **No code behaviour changed** — three comments and one test name only. Phase 41's "57 tests" is a stale figure; Phase 44 added 25.

 **THE SENTENCE THE PHASE EXISTS FOR, and it must not be softened in any later summary.** Everything built so far is TypeScript or browser JavaScript. **WordPress runs PHP. None of it runs in PHP.** Reading (b) meant the existing work _connects_; reading (a) — which Lakhbir chose — means it is **rebuilt, wrapped or dropped**. Those are different quotes, and **a developer who is shown 862 passing tests and is not told this will price the smaller one.** The decision is not reopened and this phase did not try to; §3.0 exists so the quote matches the decision.

 **The number that makes the scope concrete:** roughly **19,500 lines of non-test executable code**, **8,500 lines of test code**, **862 passing assertions across three harnesses** — all three re-run and reproduced on 1 September (site **376/0/4**, phase3 **349/0**, phase9 **137/0**, node v24.16.0). Against that, roughly **12,000 lines of Markdown** — the eleven rulebooks and the Module/Build-Prep specifications — **carry over untouched.** §12 item 24 says why that is an asset rather than a saving: **a rebuilt engine tested only against the old engine's outputs reproduces the old engine's mistakes with new confidence.**

 **THE HALF OF THE DECISION THAT DOES NOT DECIDE ITSELF, and it is W1.** "The custom back end holds the uploads" names the component that owns the files. **It says nothing about where the bytes sit.** A custom back end that writes to `wp-content/uploads/` because that is the convenient path has satisfied the decision and defeated the control — that directory is served by the web server **with no authorisation check of any kind**. A purpose-built back end need not behave like the Media Library, **but only if the brief says so**, which is why W1 is stated as a requirement with tests rather than left as answered question Q51.

 **"DPO will log" is the tamper-EVIDENT answer, and the difference is the control.** A log in the WordPress database is editable by every administrator including the record of their own actions. The determination — _the log is evidence of what happened, not proof against an administrator who alters it; administrators are trusted_ — is now a governance document rather than a line in a developer brief. **Its condition C-1 is NOT MET: nobody has enumerated the administrators, and the account is understood to be shared with several unrelated businesses.** Until that list exists, "administrators are trusted" names nobody. DPIA v2.0 R9 already says the same thing about itself, so **if C-1 is not closed before go-live, R9 is not a Medium.**

 **THE BACKUP QUESTION IS STILL OPEN AND THE WORDPRESS DECISION DID NOT ANSWER IT.** B1, item **12949133180**, now with an owner and a date. It goes to **the host or the developer — whoever controls the hosting**. The answer most likely to be misheard is _"we keep backups for 30 days"_: that is **not a yes**, it is a no with a number attached, and the number then has to be tested against the retention determination. **Nothing about client uploads should be built before the answer exists in writing.**

 **Two defects found and corrected while doing this, both of the same shape — a document telling a developer something that stopped being true.**

1.  **Developer Brief §12 item 14** said _"no upload handler exists anywhere in the codebase"_ and cited **287 passing tests**. Both were true on 30 August; neither has been true since **31 August**, when Phase 53 built the handler (919 lines, 38 tests) and phase3 reached 349. **§12 is the list a developer reads to find out what is missing**, so a stale entry there reads as a live gap — and this one contradicted §3.0.5 three sections earlier. What is still true is the part that matters: nothing calls the handler, so the controls are **dormant, not absent**.

2.  **DPIA v2.0 Gate C** said B1 blocks **"S3 only"**. The same document says at §4.2 that B1 _"covers both prefixes, and the quarantine prefix is the more urgent"_ — the row was written before B1 was widened and was not brought forward with it. **It understated the blocker, and it understated the more urgent half:** S0 holds the file unredacted, including material there is no lawful basis to hold at all, for what is meant to be about an hour. Recorded as a dated correction note under the gates table rather than by editing the row.

 **The question this phase raised rather than answered, and it moves the number more than anything else: can the hosting run a Node process?** New item **12949372270**, Developer Brief §12 item 23. If it can, ~19,500 lines are **wrapped** and 862 tests stay alive as the acceptance suite. If it cannot, **every WRAP in §3.0.2 becomes REBUILD** — including `ledgerstone-client-doc-ingestion.ts`, 1,809 lines whose correctness is measured against a legal analysis rather than an output. **Ask it in the same email as B1, and before the quote rather than after.**

 **No code was changed and no test was touched.** The three harnesses were run to verify the figures the brief now publishes, not to alter them.

Surveyor pack (doc 46592069): I1–I5 carry the answer, I6 the explanation. **A preamble was added before Section 1 / Question 1 in each**, so the reader meets the convention before the first question |
|  **2 — the two corrections** |  **H4 marked as answering the wrong half** — which date, not whose purchase. **H8 marked PARTIALLY ANSWERED** — correct general rule, not the narrower point. Both recorded in the pack itself, not only on the board |
|  **3 — engine changes** |  **I4:** quantity model to **v3** — room-driven promoted from one row's fix to the model's standing default; RD-04 split into RD-04a (room-driven, cellular) and RD-04b (area density, open-plan). **I5:** `LS_P9_WORKING_METHOD` added to the cost model with five tests |
|  **4 — what still goes to the surveyor** |  New **§1A** in the call agenda: I1/I2 stay because a commercial preference is not the answer asked for; the no-minimum-job-size consequence stated; **I4 and I5 to be put as a pair** |
|  **Switch table** |  **Unchanged. All ten verified still ****`false`**** by parsing the source**, not by memory. Note added to both the switch-table document and the source, saying why |

 **THE CAUTION HELD, AND IT WAS LIVE RATHER THAN THEORETICAL.** Three of the four tax answers **agreed with our own reading**, which is exactly the circumstance in which flipping a switch feels like housekeeping. The pack's opening sentence — _we are not looking for someone to bless an aggressive position we have already taken_ — **would have become false the moment any of them went on.** Nothing went on. Every answer is recorded as **the company's provisional position, pending the adviser's confirmation**, and is labelled that way in every box.

 **THE FINDING THAT CHANGES WHAT DELIVERABLE 3 COULD MEAN, and the next phase should not re-derive it.** The instruction said the I4 change would move output values and to expect calibration figures to shift. **It did not, and could not: there is no code anywhere in this project that derives a device quantity.** The S9 model is a specification, all fifteen coefficients are blank by design, and `quantity` is schema-fixed at grade D pending a surveyor's signature. Grepping for the coefficient ids and for `LS-MP-003` across every `.ts`, `.cjs` and `.html` returns nothing. **So I4 is a specification change, the harness could not move, and an unchanged harness here is the correct result rather than evidence the edit did nothing.** That is written into the model at §0A.3 so it is not re-litigated.

 **WHERE I4 WAS APPLIED AND WHERE IT WAS DELIBERATELY NOT.** v2 had already fixed detectors (RD-01) and common parts (RD-13). The instruction named **data points and light fittings** as having the same shape. **Data points: half true.** The model's own §6b refused the room-driven substitution for two reasons, and only one of them survives. _A published standard exists and states a figure_ stands untouched — **RD-04 is still closed by a purchase, not by judgement.** But _the mix is genuinely unknown_ is an argument against replacing the coefficient, **not** an argument for leaving it as a single area density — because one area figure silently assumes the building is 100% open-plan, which in a clinical building is the assumption already known to be wrong. **Splitting it makes the mix a question somebody must answer rather than an assumption nobody notices.** Both halves stay blank. **Light fittings: not true at all.** There is no general-lighting coefficient in any form — RD-15 is _emergency_ lighting and is blocked behind taxonomy gap XS-1. **So general lighting was never modelled rather than modelled wrongly**, and that is now recorded as a gap (§0A.2) with the rule that if the row is ever added it is written room-driven from birth.

 **I5 WAS RECORDED WITHOUT BEING MADE TRUE, and the distinction is the whole of the work.** `LS_P9_WORKING_METHOD` states whole-building ageing, who said it, when, and on what question. It is explicitly **not the default** (`DEPRECIATION_METHOD_DEFAULT` stays `NONE`, because inaction must not become a decision), **not surveyor-set** (Lakhbir is the controller; the `DEPRECIATION_METHOD_NOT_SET_BY_SURVEYOR` flag still fires and is correct), and **not effective** (the E5b gate is blocked on the VOA obsolescence licence — a purchase, not an opinion). **Five tests hold exactly those three properties**, so a later phase cannot quietly promote it.

 **THE PAIRING IS THE THING TO CARRY TO THE CALL.** I4 buys **more** precision in counting; I5 accepts **less** in ageing. That may be right — counting is cheap once a room list exists, whereas per-element ageing needs plant lives we do not hold and would be false precision stacked on estimated quantities. **But it is a combination, and putting either half to the surveyor without the other invites an answer to the wrong question.** It is written into the call agenda, the cost-model source and the surveyor pack, in those terms.

 **A MISTAKE THIS PHASE MADE, caught by the harness within a minute.** The note added above `LS_CTA` cited the switch-table document **by filename** — which carries the legacy brand — and Suite M's "the site carries no legacy brand name" assertion failed immediately. **Fixed by naming the document without the literal string.** The guard Phase 49 built did its job on the phase that was not thinking about it.

# PHASE 64 — DONE, 2 September 2026 (PharmaAdmin). The Scotland answer is priced, and it cost three live defects. Prompt deleted.


 The instruction section is deleted, per the convention.

 **HARNESS TOTALS: site 392 pass / 0 fail / 4 xfail** (was 377/0/4 — fifteen new tests, suite N, no regressions) **· phase3 349/0** unchanged **· phase9 142/0** untouched.

 **DELIVERABLE: Jurisdiction Matrix v1** — board item **12954958944**, Monday doc **18429306463**, disk copy `02-modules-and-build-prep\Ledgerstone-Jurisdiction-Matrix-v1.md`. Nine data dependencies × **four** jurisdictions, each with source, whether it exists, what it costs and the fallback; then the sequencing recommendation.

 **THE BRIEF'S PREMISE WAS RIGHT AND ITS EMPHASIS WAS WRONG, in both directions.** It expected the rate table to be the problem and the coverage claim to be the easy fix. In fact the **Scottish rate table was already built and verified** — `SCOTLAND_BY_YEAR`, six bands, `uninc_scot [0.19, 0.48]`, Rulebook I Addendum 1, done on 25 August. Nothing needed doing there. What was broken was one layer down: **the engine did not reliably know it was in Scotland.**

 **THREE LIVE DEFECTS, all in the shipped file, all now closed.**

 **1. Two sectors read ****`s.is_scotland`**** and no question ever set it.** `dental` and `supported_living` both compute `rateKey = s.claimant_type==="company" ? "company" : (s.is_scotland ? "uninc_scot" : "uninc_ruk")`, and neither engine had a nation question anywhere in its `Q[]`. `s.is_scotland` was permanently `undefined` — falsy — so **every Scottish unincorporated dental practice and supported-living provider was silently valued at rUK rates.** 45% where the answer is 48% at the top, and wrong in both directions across six bands against four. This is the shape of defect a harness cannot catch by counting: both halves of the code were individually correct and nothing connected them.

 **2. The three sectors that did ask, asked the wrong people.** `care_homes` Q1a and `private_hospital` H1b carried `showIf: ["sole_trader","partnership","llp"].includes(s.claimant_type)`, because the question had been written as a RATES question. **Nation is also a SOURCING question** — whether HM Land Registry covers the property does not depend on how the claimant is taxed — so companies, the majority of claimants, were never asked which nation they were in at all.

 **3. The site made no coverage claim, which reads as all of it.** Fixed first, before the research, per the brief.

 **THE FIX: ****`LS_JURIS`****, one new module in the ****`LS_`**** shared layer.** `SERVED = { england:true, wales:true, scotland:false, ni:false }` is the whole switch, one line. **It is deliberately NOT a CTA switch** — no tax position turns on it; it is a statement about our own operational coverage, so it is Lakhbir's to flip, not the adviser's. One shared nation question replaces the three divergent ones and is added to the two sectors that had none, asked of every claimant, offering all four nations rather than a Scotland/rest binary. An unserved nation hits a gate that is **a route, not a refusal**: it says the relief exists there and the limit is our tool, then offers the manual service. `LS_JURIS.SOURCES` encodes the matrix so the engine already knows what it cannot derive in a nation rather than discovering it in front of a client.

 **THE COPY CANNOT DRIFT FROM THE FLAG.** Test **N7** asserts that the published sentence on the marketing page matches `LS_JURIS.servedPhrase()`. Flip `SERVED` without touching the site and the harness fails. Test **N2** is the regression guard for defect 1: _no sector may read __`s.is_scotland`__ unless a question in that sector sets it._

 **THE RECOMMENDATION, AND THE FINDING THAT COMPLICATES IT.** Launch **England and Wales, then Scotland, then Northern Ireland**. But the obvious fallback is **not free**: Wales shares the property registers with England yet has **HIW absent from the source register entirely**, **CIW registered with ****`endpoint: null`**, and **Rulebook F's GP grant rules are NHS England's**. England and Wales is still right — the Welsh gaps are corroboration and grant-catalogue gaps that degrade gracefully to client answers, whereas the Scottish and NI gap is the _primary derivation_, the purchase price — but it is a boundary with three named holes, not a clean one. **Northern Ireland is the hardest of the three, not the smallest:** no open price-paid data at any price, only £5.00 per folio under the Land Registry (Fees) Order (NI) 2010.

 **THE ESCALATION, per the brief's instruction.** Only one item turned out to need a rulebook rather than a data-source swap, and it is **not** the one expected. **The fixtures regime does NOT need a Scottish rulebook** — CAA 2001 writes its Scottish equivalents into its own text (s.175(1) "or, in Scotland, lease"; s.175(3) has its own Scottish limb). What does need a tax answer is **which date starts the clock in a Scottish transaction** — missives, date of entry or registration of the disposition — because our s.187A clocks and the two-year s.198 window are written against English exchange/completion language. **Q73, to the CTA.**

 **Rulebook F is England-only in substance** — NHS (GMS – Premises Costs) Directions 2024 are NHS England's, and Homes England / SAHP / GLA are England-only funders. But the _tax_ rule (ss.532–538, public-body payer kills the s.536 exception) travels intact; what is England-only is the **catalogue of payers**. So that is research-and-drafting per nation, **not** a CTA question and not a new regime.

 **FOUR NEW QUESTIONS — Q72–Q75**, all with recommendations, in DECISIONS Part 15 (doc 46592292, now v16.0). Q72 the launch scope; Q73 the CTA date question; Q74 the Registers of Scotland API tariff, which they do not publish and someone has to ask; Q75 whether a £5-per-folio NI lookup is acceptable or NI runs on client figures.

 **ONE CORRECTION MADE IN PASSING, unrelated to jurisdiction.** The source register's EPC endpoint was `epc.opendatacommunities.org`; the service moved to `get-energy-performance-data.communities.gov.uk` on **30 May 2026** and the old host now 301s. Fixed in `phase3/ledgerstone-source-register.ts`, phase3 still 349/0.

 **WHAT WAS DELIBERATELY NOT DONE.** The seven new sources (RoS, Scottish EPC, Care Inspectorate, SAA, RQIA, LPS NI, LRNI) were **not** added to `phase3/ledgerstone-source-register.ts`. Registering them means asserting a licence and redistribution position for each, which is exactly what Q74/Q75 exist to answer — and that file's whole job is to be the licence authority, so putting guessed terms in it would be the defect it exists to prevent. `LS_JURIS.SOURCES` names them all so nothing is lost.

 **Backups** (`.bak-phase64`) taken for `ledgerstone-site.html`, `ledgerstone-regression.cjs` and `phase3/ledgerstone-source-register.ts`.

 **Phases 65, 66 and 67 are all DONE (2 Sep)****, and the Phase 68 sweep has now run** — its completion record is below. **Phase 69 remains**: finishing the data-holding reversal across the whole board corpus, because Phase 68 found three asserting instances in the live decision list that Phase 60's count of fourteen never included. **The sweep is now Pha****s****e 70 and stays last****.** Two things it should still carry: Q76 (the privacy notice that unblocks the derivation layer, item 12955356558) and Q55, which remains the one decision blocking work.

### The three things the answer did not do, which is why this was a phase and not a setting

 **1. It produced no deletion date.** `RETAIN_FOR_DEFENCE_PERIOD` reads a date supplied by the defence-pack clock RET-1 — an unset blank whose drafting defect is itself open as Q60. Selected and left there, "keep it" is **indefinite retention arrived at by omission**; test R9 has surfaced that since Phase 44, and it is exactly what a one-line configuration change would have shipped. **RET-7 is now the clock and is deliberately switched off** (`settings.ret7_approved` defaults false), because a derived period is not an approved one. **Approving RET-7 is now on the critical path for accepting uploads at all** — new board item for the DPO.

 **2. It does not reach every document.** A document whose strip removed `NO_LAWFUL_BASIS` content cannot go on the long clock — condition D4 — and is deleted on the extraction clock. **So we will delete some client documents despite an instruction to keep them.** Retention Determinations §7.3 said a Reading B answer changes "one sentence and no arithmetic": right about the arithmetic, one sentence short.

 **3. It changed the premise Q45 rests on.** Q45 (fund the redaction producer) is recommended "not now" **because deleting the original held less data, so waiting cost nothing**. We no longer delete it, and `CONDITION_D4_STATUS` gives exactly two routes to meeting D4 for a kept file — the answer closed the first. The recommendation may still be "not now"; it cannot still be for that reason. **Annotated, not reopened.**

### The defect found by switching promotion on

 Under the old default the raw file **never reached durable storage**. Reading B switches promotion on, and `shouldPromoteRawFile` took only the settings while the retention clock is **per document** — so it would have promoted the D4-affected class too, writing the `REPRESENTATIONS`, `CONSULTEE_RESPONSES` and `CORRESPONDENCE` that N3 records as **unlawful to hold** into the six-year store, to delete them moments later. **The stated rule was already right; it was being applied to the settings instead of to the document.** Found by building the answer, not by reviewing it.

### One correction to a claim made two hours earlier in this same phase

 The first draft of the DPIA amendment said R10's ordinary case was **"narrowed"** by the longer clock. It is not. The false-record exposure is the length of the backup rotation and it opens at the deletion event whenever that event happens — **deferred by six years, not narrowed**. Corrected the same day at DPIA §A2.5, and the consequence for B1 is written out at Dashboard Data Specification Amendment 1: **two of B1's three cases still need the exclusion limb, and they are the two carrying content there is no lawful basis to hold. "Our backups only go back thirty days" is not an answer to B1.**

### What was checked and found stale rather than assumed

 Q56's own text warned that keeping a copy "cuts against the answers you gave on holding data". **Written before Phase 60 and now wrong** — the 1 September answers moved client personal data into the back end deliberately. And the brief's hoped-for upside, that redaction would shrink the Article 14 notification population, **was never available**: since Phase 60 the names sit in the identity store by design, and holding them is what makes the duty performable. **The real upside is different and smaller: Article 14(2)(a) can now be answered with a period and criteria instead of "as long as necessary".**

# PHASE 75 — DONE, 4 September 2026 (PharmaAdmin). Prompt deleted. The first outside evidence this project has had. Four surveyor questions answered by worked example, one live under-claim found in every purchase claim we produce, and sixteen answers recorded as provisional with every switch still off. 

 Two parts ran. The **Eureka Capital Allowances** client deliverable in `Desktop\reports` was extracted and benchmarked against our method; and Lakhbir's sixteen answers of 3 September were transcribed into the two specialist packs. Full record in **Decisions Document 3, Part 22 (v23.0)**. Items **12966924103** and **12966924104**, both Done, claims cleared.

### What the benchmark settled

 Four things that had been sitting as surveyor questions now have a worked competitor answer: **the valuation basis** (replacement cost for plant and building, open market value for the bare site — two bases in one formula); **the planning assumption** (existing type of development, and stated on the face of the report, which answers both halves of that question); **indexation** (brought back to the date of purchase, though the column is nil on this job, so the question becomes _which_ index); and **what the report must contain** (seven parts, not our twenty — what makes it defensible is statutory citation by section, express findings on s.185 and s.187A, and a chain where every figure is cross-referenced both ways). It also answers Lakhbir's own question back: **BCIS, not Spon's.**

### The finding of the phase

 **SDLT is inside the competitor's apportionable base, and it is not inside ours.** The funnel captures the purchase price only; the sole occurrence of the concept in our code returns the _name_ of the tax and never an amount. **And the engine already tells non-England clients that "acquisition costs added to the base under s.562 are LTT, not SDLT"** — asserting a behaviour the arithmetic does not perform. Understatement is exactly T/(P+T): 4.76% on their job, ~4.1% on a £1.5m care home, on **every purchase claim we produce**. Not fixed — the fix makes claims bigger. **New item 12975610449, question Q86, for the CTA.**

### The finding that changes an existing item

 **LEG-E2's mechanism is confirmed and its premise is now in doubt.** Stripping the 18% and 15% takes their plant claim from £73,740 to £66,325 — +11.2% — and the overstatement rises with land fraction exactly as our Phase 9 note predicted. But the premise ("on-costs are already inside estimated replacement cost") is about a **VOA cost book**, and Eureka prices on **BCIS elemental rates, where preliminaries sit outside the unit rates**. On that source the 18% is not a double count. **LEG-E2's real gate is which price book the model assumes — a surveyor question, not the VOA licence. Q87. Not shipped.** LEG-E3 is unchanged and its block stands.

### What was flagged rather than filed

 **The care home / supported living answer — "claim for everything, you do not have to restrict" — contradicts defect E-1, shipped 20 August, which removed shared lounges, kitchens and resident bathrooms from the claimable base on CA11520.** The engine has not been widened. E-1 stands. It is put to both the adviser and the surveyor as the question it is, split into four cases, with the conflict stated on the face of both packs and recorded on the E-1 item.

 **The two-year clock was answered with the date again, not the person — the third time this half has been answered.** Recorded as still open, and the pack now says so in terms.

 **Connected-party contributions: "use your understanding" is not an answer**, and it is the reading that makes claims bigger. Not built. It stays with the adviser.

# PHASE 77 — DONE, 4 September 2026 (PharmaAdmin). The comparison is built, computed on every call and returned; both switches are OFF. The finding is far bigger than the competitor invoice: for EVERY company client the fee exceeds the year-one benefit at ANY pool split, and no split fixes it. 

 The instruction section is deleted, per the convention.

 **HARNESS TOTALS, re-derived per suite, not inherited:** site **563 pass / 0 fail / 4 xfail** (was 503 — suite R adds 60), `phase3` **358 / 0** across ten files, `phase9` **142 / 0** across three, both untouched. `node 03-app/ledgerstone-figure-drift.cjs` green after five stale 503s were corrected. Backups `.bak-phase77` taken for `Caprebate site.html` and `ledgerstone-regression.cjs`.

 **WHAT WAS BUILT.** `LS_BENEFIT`, a realised-benefit model beside the fee module, and `LS_FEEGUARD`, two switches on the LS_CTA build-then-sign-off pattern. `LS_RATES` gained the first-year relief rates (AIA, its £1m limit, full expensing, the 50% FYA, and the new s.45U 40% FYA) because Rulebook I rule 7.1 says the rate table is the only place this application may state a rate — restating them inside the benefit model would have been LEG-E1's five-copies defect, one phase after it was fixed.

 **WHAT DID NOT CHANGE, AND IS ASSERTED NOT TO HAVE.** The fee rate (5%), the basis (allowances identified, Q55), and the disclosure — byte-identical, pinned against a literal in test R7. With both switches off the rendered amount is what shipped. Nothing a client sees changed in this phase.

 **THE COMPARISON IS RETURNED ON EVERY CALL**, switches or no switches, including the refusal path where the fee itself is null — with `computed:false` and a reason rather than an absent field. That was the point of the phase: a figure that exists is a figure someone can act on.

 **THE COMPETITOR CASE REPRODUCES EXACTLY.** Fed Eureka's real numbers (main £34,075, special £39,665, 40%, first period 2022/23) the model returns their published writing-down schedule line for line — £6,134 / £5,029 / £4,124 / £3,382 main, £2,380 / £2,237 / £2,103 / £1,977 special. Year five is ours and not theirs, deliberately: FA 2026 moved the main pool to 14% and their 2024 report predates it. Our fee £3,687.00 against a year-one benefit of £3,405.36 — **short by £281.64**. Fed their client's actual profits the model returns their reported £1,010.00 repayment exactly, against which our fee is 3.65×.

 **THE FINDING THAT IS NOT ABOUT ONE INVOICE.** Year-one relief is (pool rate × tax rate) of allowances; our fee is a flat 5% of the same base. A company's best possible case is 18% × 26.5% = **4.77%**. **There is no pool split, at any rate, at which a company client's fee does not exceed their year-one benefit.** Same for a basic-rate sole trader. Only higher-rate and above unincorporated clients clear it, and from April 2026 a 40% client needs **82% of the claim in the main pool** to do so — healthcare fit-outs are usually the other way round. It is a timing problem, not a value problem: over five years the fee is 29% of the benefit on the Eureka case.

 **ESCALATED, NOT DECIDED — Q90 and Q91, in DECISIONS Part 24 (doc 46592292, now v25.0).** Q90: cap, warn, or adjust the percentage. Recommendation is warn plus adjust — the model computes `breakeven_fee_rate_year_one`, the rate at which the fee stops exceeding the year-one benefit on that client's facts (4.62% on the Eureka case), which is exactly what the percentage conversation Lakhbir described needs. Q91: `aia_headroom` and `sufficient_profit` are read by `LS_CASH` and captured by no question in any of the five flows, so no first-year relief can ever be modelled and the profits constraint can never be applied. Two questions would fix both.

 **WHAT WAS DELIBERATELY NOT DONE.** No switch turned on, including the two created. No entitlement invented — `reliefsEstablished()` returns nothing established on every case the shipped question set can produce, and says which fact is missing. Where a fact is unknown the model returns a bounded RANGE and the fee-exceeds boolean stays three-valued rather than guessing. The disclosure was not reworded.

 **A negative control was run** — perturbing the main-pool rate turns 14 of the 60 assertions red, and flipping a switch in the file turns 3 red — so the suite is evidence and not decoration.

## Phase 83 — Clean up the board: names, order, and the comment clutter. DONE, 4 September 2026

 **Scope decision, stated first because it shapes every number below.** Parts A and B were run across the **112 live items** in groups 00 to 05. **Group Z (198 items) was deliberately left alone.** Part A says "every LIVE item"; group Z is titled Complete / Not Applicable, and Part B expressly protects its updates as the historical record. Renaming an archive destroys the record of what a finished thing was called — the same harm Part A's own "the reasoning is not deleted, it is moved" rule exists to prevent. This is a decision, not an omission.

 **Headline: 89 renamed · 24 updates removed · 4 runs condensed into 4 replacements · 7 owner-type or status retags · 1 kept because I could not tell.**

 The phase's premise was that items sit on three template labels. **They do not, and that had to be checked rather than assumed.** A filtered query for items on labels 0/1/2 returned zero; a second query (`not_any_of [3,4,6,7,8,9]`) confirmed it independently and found the real gap — **three items with no owner type at all**, all in group Z: Market & competitor research, Secure startup funding, Dev meeting (Back end).  The three dead labels — "Working on it", "Done", "Stuck" — were then **removed from ****`color_mm6bhs21`**. Nothing was orphaned because nothing sat on them. Read back: six labels remain, and a post-removal `not_any_of` query returns zero items.

 Board ids, Q-numbers, defect codes, version numbers and dates are out of every live name. **Prefixes were kept only where they earn it**: the three `SURVEYOR · STEP n of 3` items, where the sequence is the point; and the seven rulebook file-holders, now `📄 FILE ONLY — Rulebook X. The Rulebook X item carries the status; deleting this deletes the rulebook`, because that warning is the entire reason those items exist.

 **Headline: 85 answer blocks, one under every question in all five sections. Six refinement tables broken up into individually answerable questions. One entry moved off the document because it was a task, not a question, and one rewritten because only part of it still asked anybody anything.**

 **Two of those counts were wrong in the document's own headers and are now corrected.** The accountant section said "twelve questions" and carried thirteen — the thirteenth is the money-laundering supervision question, which is addressed to whoever does the accountant's own compliance rather than to the accountant, which is presumably how it fell out of the count. The developer section said "six questions" and carried five, and now carries four. The summary table at the top of the document had both wrong figures and now shows the corrected ones plus a total row.

### Part A — the answer block

 The block is **identical on all 85 questions**, rendered as a fixed-width panel so the dotted rules and the columns hold their shape:

```
ANSWER
......................................................................
Your answer:

How confident are you?    High / Medium / Low
Answered by:                                     Date:
If you disagree with our recommendation, what should we do instead?
......................................................................
```

 **It sits under the question it answers, before the divider, every time** — never in a table at the end. A person answers where they are reading.

 **Three supporting changes to the front of the document,** because a form nobody understands is not an improvement:

-  The document's own contract — "every question below carries five things" — now says **six**, with "an answer block: somewhere to write the answer, on the question itself" as the sixth row.

-  A new **How to answer** paragraph: click into the box and type between the dotted lines; nothing needs sending back separately and nobody has to transcribe it.

-  A paragraph explaining why two of the lines are there rather than being politeness. **Confidence changes what we do with the answer** — on a tax reading, "high" means we switch a branch on and "medium" means we build it and leave it off, so please undersell rather than oversell. And **the disagree line exists because four recorded answers so far have answered a slightly different question from the one asked**; the line invites the correction rather than making the reader volunteer it.

### The refinement questions — the structural half of the work

Nobody had to decide anything: it described work for us to do, and it was already on the board as its own task at _Ready - Claude can build_. **No second board item was created.** The full text of the entry was written onto that task as an update before it was deleted here, so nothing is lost, and a **one-line pointer** stays at the end of the developer section telling a developer that the two new client questions are specified on the task rather than in this document.

So the entry is now the question that was actually outstanding — **"Who exactly can administer the website — and does that include the host's own staff?"** — with the settled decisions stated in one line as context. The board item that carries C-1 was updated to say the question is now answerable in the questions document.

One entry — the note that the outgoing Accountant Handover Pack still carries the old brand name — is a task and is on the board, but it is explicitly labelled "one thing to fix before any of this goes out" rather than posed as a question, and it warns whoever is about to send the pack, so it was left as a note.

### The two standing checks

-  **Answerable cold.** The refinement questions gained the most here: as table rows they leaned on a column header for their framing, and each now carries its own context sentence.

-  **No board ids and no Q-numbers in the body.** Re-checked against the finished document by pattern search: **zero** matches for either.

### One finding that lands on Phase 87, and it has been written into that phase's prompt

 **Markdown export does not round-trip bold and italic** for text written through the API. The stored delta is correct — every run carries the same attribute, so Monday displays it properly — but the exporter emits one marker pair _per run_, so a bolded phrase comes out as `**T****h****at senten****c****e**`. It is invisible in the product and disfiguring in a file. Phase 87 exports 169 documents to disk, so it would have baked this into every one of them. Its prompt now says to export one document first, look at a paragraph known to be bolded, and decide whether to post-process before doing the rest.

### Not done

 **NOTHING LEFT.** Parts A and B are complete across all five sections, and the export-fidelity finding has a home in Phase 87's prompt rather than in prose.

## An API trap that cost four failed calls, now in COORDINATES

 **`add_markdown_content`**** fails with a bare "Internal server error" when ****`after_block_id`**** names a block that is not top-level.** Four calls failed in a row — at 6.4KB, 3.3KB and then at 500 bytes — which looked exactly like the recorded payload-size and block-count ceilings and is neither. **The anchor was a text block inside a table cell.** The ids returned by a previous `add_markdown_content` include every cell and cell-child it created, so the LAST id in that list is usually nested, and using it as the next anchor fails. **Take the anchor from a fresh read, filtered to ****`parent_block_id === null`****.** The one-line test that distinguishes this from the size ceilings: append a tiny chunk with **no** anchor — if that lands, the importer is fine and the anchor is the problem.

 **Also confirmed, and it contradicts an earlier note:** deleting a table block **does** delete its cells and their children. 38 top-level deletions removed 190 blocks and left zero orphans. But a batch that names cell ids **explicitly** is rejected with `BAD_USER_INPUT` — so delete the table, never its cells.
