### Findings worth keeping

-  **The item-id-plus-title filename is not unique, and the failure is silent.** An item can hold three documents (`doc_mm6b6y15`, `doc_mm6nrqrn`, `doc_mm6p2bcx`) and two of them can share a heading. Fixed in the tooling, but the class of bug — a naming scheme that looks unique and is not — is worth remembering.

-  **Phase History does not live in 00 START HERE.** It sits in group Z. A scope defined as "every group except 00 START HERE" would have swept it up and destroyed it. Excluding the five hub documents **by id**, as the prompt required, is what saved it — the group-based reading would not have.

-  **Presigned upload URLs really do expire in fifteen minutes**, whatever `url_expires_at` says — that field reported 24 hours while `X-Amz-Expires` said 900 seconds, and the signature is what counts. Two uploads failed 403 on that. Separately, three failed **400** in a single batch, all sharing one STS credential that had expired independently of the signature. In both cases a fresh URL fixed it immediately.

-  **The exporter rate-limits.** A 24-document batch came back with nine 429s. The tooling treats a failed export as RETRY rather than a permanent skip, so they were simply picked up by the next batch — no intervention needed.

-  **`net::ERR_NETWORK_IO_SUSPENDED`**** appeared three times** and cleared on an immediate retry each time. It is the same failure that ended the earlier run; it is transient and not a reason to stop.

-  **Large aliased export queries are the efficient shape.** Twenty-four `export_markdown_from_doc` aliases in one call return the whole batch, and the payload is big enough that the result is written to a file instead of passing through context. Batches of eight came back inline and could not be piped to the parser — bigger batches are actually easier, not harder.

### Tooling

 `_tools/p87.cjs`, `_tools/fixmd.cjs` and `_tools/put2.sh` in `08-monday-doc-exports` are the durable copies. `put2.sh` takes complete presigned URLs on a TSV line rather than reassembling them from parts, which removes the hardcoded date the earlier script carried.

### What the grep actually found, and why the prompt understated it

 The prompt named two board items as carrying the old name. The real figure, derived by grepping the whole export folder rather than trusting those two: **204 of 227 files, 2,036 occurrences.** The two named items account for a handful of them. Nothing was inherited; every number here was re-derived from disk.

### The classification, because a blanket swap would have been wrong

 The board group is the primary signal for whether a document is live, but it is **not sufficient**, and this is the finding worth carrying forward. Group Z holds two completely different kinds of thing: genuine engineering history ("F-2 over-claim — completed") and **legal instruments whose drafting task is finished but which are in force today** — the governance policies, the breach register, the rights-request pack, the Article 14 assessment, the DPO instrument. Renaming the first kind would falsify a record; leaving the second kind would leave live legal documents under a dead company name. 130 files were changed and 63 deliberately left.

 Four classes of string were protected and did not move:

-  **`ledgerstone.co.uk`**** / ****`ledgerstone.com`** — these belong to a different, trading business. The sentence exists to say the old name is taken. Three of these survive inside changed documents, which is correct.

-  **Two documents whose subject IS the old name** — the professional-email-and-brand first pass (it is the naming study) and the ASA/CAP Code claim audit (it quotes the old site copy verbatim as evidence; altering a quotation marked "exact" would falsify it).

-  **The former folder names ****`Ledgestone all/ledgerstone all`** — a real filesystem fact inside directory inventories. Correcting these is re-pathing, not renaming, and the two differ. Left alone and carried forward.

-  **Engineering tickets titled "Ledgerstone — Fix/Model/Add/Make/Derive…"** — eight of these were swapped by mistake because the history regex expected a space where the titles use an em dash. Caught on review, reverted from backup, 26 swaps undone.

### The Phase 87 conclusion that was wrong

 Phase 87 recorded that the Monday API has no way to remove an asset from a column, and left two fragmented files attached to the surveyor item for manual deletion. **It does have one.** `update_assets_on_item(board_id, item_id, column_id, files:[{assetId, fileType: asset, name}])` sets the column to exactly the list given and drops everything else. Tested end to end on one low-stakes file before being used at scale.

 That matters twice over. It is why no item is sitting with a Caprebate copy and a Ledgerstone copy side by side, and it closed Phase 87's own carry-forward: the surveyor item now holds three correctly named files and the fragmented duplicates are gone.

 **The trap in it:** Monday re-creates the assets on every such call, so the asset ids change. Read the column immediately before writing it; never reuse an id from an earlier read.

-  **Every engine module reference in the exported documents is stale.** 55 files carry `LS_CTA`, `LS_POOL`, `LS_ELECTION` and so on; **zero carry ****`CB_`**. Phase 78 renamed all 18 prefixes on disk and the disk now has zero `LS_` in markdown. The exported documents never got the change. Swapped in the 130 changed files; the 63 historical ones keep `LS_` on purpose.

Their filenames are visible to the adviser.

 **Verified rather than assumed.** Two documents were downloaded back from the board and compared byte-for-byte against the renamed copies on disk. The Accountant Handoff Pack — the outgoing document the prompt called the most urgent single instance — now reads Caprebate thirteen times and Ledgerstone zero. The Breach and Transparency pack matches its disk copy exactly and retains one Ledgerstone: the `ledgerstone.co.uk` sentence, which is protected on purpose.

 **What the second half of the run added to the first.** The mechanism, the classification and the eight reverted engineering tickets are recorded in the mid-run entry above and are unchanged. Three things are new:

-  **The de-duplication is complete, not partial.** Every one of the 108 touched items was read immediately before it was written — necessary, because `update_assets_on_item` re-creates the assets and invalidates every id from an earlier read. Items holding files this phase never touched (the Module 00 specification, the strawman schedules, the six older rulebook attachments, the journey wireframe) kept them; they were listed explicitly in each write rather than left to chance.

-  **STS credentials rotate faster than a long run survives.** The credential pool turned over roughly every few calls and each token expires in 900 seconds, so `_tools/tokens.tsv` has to be rebuilt per batch. Carrying it across a session break produces signature failures that look like permission errors.

-  **Zero upload failures across 128 files.** None of Phase 87's reported failure modes — the 403s on expired presigned URLs, the 400s on independently expired STS credentials, the 429s, the transient network suspensions — recurred, because no URL was held longer than the few seconds between issuing it and using it.

 **Carried into Phase 92, and nothing is left as prose.** The seven rulebook attachments still named `Ledgerstone-Statutory-Rules-Register-…` (uploaded as files, never documents, so unreachable by an export-based rename); the stale `Ledgestone all` folder paths in six live documents; and the three data-protection documents still asserting the public notices page is blocked behind Q3 when Q3 is answered and the domain is live. Phase 92 carries the evidence for each, including which documents to leave alone and why.

 **Escalated, not decided.** The tax implication summaries, the accountant cover note and letter, the CTA decision pack and the rulebooks are client-facing **and** carry tax content. The brand fix on them is finished; **the tax content still waits on the appointed adviser and none of them is ready to send.** Recorded in FOR THE ACCOUNTANT rather than left in a phase record.

### Three API facts worth keeping, all written into COORDINATES

-  **`blocks`**** comes back in ID order, not document order, and pagination follows that order.** A section near the end of a document can land on page 1 and a section near the middle on page 3. Every block carries a `position`; concatenate all pages and sort on it. Anchoring an insert on an array index puts text in the wrong place.

-  **A table cell holds no text of its own.** Its text is in a child block whose `parent_block_id` is the cell id. To change one number in a table, update the child — updating the cell does nothing. This is how the counts table was corrected without rebuilding it.

-  **`create_column`**** for a status column wants ****`labels`**** as an ARRAY of ****`{label, index, color}`**** with an integer colour.** An object map, or a hex string, is rejected with a schema error that does not name the right shape.

 Also recorded: the shipped engine is `Caprebate site.html` at the **Desktop root**, one level above the Caprebate folder — searching the project tree for it returns only archived forks — and the node binary is inside the versioned folder, `node-portable/node-v24.16.0-win-x64/node.exe`; `node-portable/node.exe` does not exist.

### The price books — the largest thing in this phase

 Four PDFs had been sitting at the folder root since 31 August. **All three tests the phase set were run, and they do not agree with each other.**

 **(a) They exist and open.** Text was extracted from all three. The existing extractor could not do it — it returned every glyph unmapped, which looks exactly like a scanned document; the ToUnicode maps were inside compressed object streams it does not expand. `pdf2txt3.cjs` adds object-stream expansion and gets 1,476,173 glyphs with **zero** unmapped on the 2022 book and 171 of 1,350,125 on the 2024 one.

 **(b) They are, in part, the right books — but for one engine fix, not three.**

|  What the board says is waiting |  Is it in these books? |
| --- | --- |
|  Location factors (`CB_LOCATION_FACTORS`) |  **Yes.** Architects' & Builders' 2024, page 49: thirteen regions, Outer London = 1.00, Inner London 1.05 to Northern Ireland 0.74. |
|  Contract size adjustment (`CB_CONTRACT_SIZE_ADJUSTMENT`) |  **Yes**, as "Adjustment According to Contract Sum Cost" — but declared valid only for projects of £2m–£5m. |
|  Professional fee scale (`CB_VOA_FEE_SCALE`) |  **No.** The book gives a benchmark mean of 2.2% on a £4m new build, expressly "not minimum or maximum values". The engine is specified against the banded **Valuation Office** scale, which is a different source with its own licence. |
|  Preliminaries (the item that needs no data at all) |  Not relevant — that item removes a multiplier. |

 **Two constraints that would make a naive implementation wrong, and one of them does not wait on the purchase.** The book says twice that its adjustments "need to be applied to the **total cost plan value**, not to individual material or element items" — and the full specification's worked example applies a Cardiff 94 factor to individual element lines. **That is a design defect in our specification, not a data gap.** And the factors are indexed to **Outer London = 1.00** while `CB_LOCATION_FACTORS` declares a **mean of 100**, with the Mechanical & Electrical book using London on a third base again. Both written onto the board items.

 **(c) And this is the finding. We should not use these particular files at all.** Every page of the 2022 Mechanical & Electrical book prints, in its own header, the path of the machine it was typeset on — a `OneDrive-Informaplc` folder under `SPON/MandE/dtp`, **816 times**. Informa plc is Taylor & Francis's parent. **That is publisher pre-press output, not a customer copy.** Both books carry the standard notice forbidding reproduction "in any information storage or retrieval system" without written permission, which is precisely what loading rate tables into the engine would be. So the commercial-use question the phase asked to be put to Lakhbir is real, but it sits behind a prior one: how did we come by these files. Both are in the questions document.

 **One earlier claim corrected.** The record said the Spon's books "contain nothing for dental practices or care homes". **Care homes are covered** — residential homes £95,000–£135,000 per bed, nursing homes £120,000–£170,000 per bed, at 40–60 m² per bedroom. Dental practices genuinely are not; every apparent match is "incidental" or "accidental".

 **The purchase item was retagged and renamed** — from `Blocked - question` to `Blocked - licence or purchase`, because the obstacle is no longer "ask the surveyor whether they subscribe". A surveyor's single-user reading licence would not cover our engine either. The blockers document said that subscription "may remove the £330 purchase entirely"; that was misleading and has been corrected in three places in it.

### The finding, and it is a document nobody had opened

 **The client engagement letter is finished. It has been since 4 September. Six live Monday documents say it does not exist, one board item asks whether it was ever written, and no solicitor has read it.**

 `06-commercial-and-governance/Caprebate Engagement Letter.docx` — 21,780 bytes, 8,448 characters of body text, **thirteen numbered clauses**: parties, scope of services (including instruction of a chartered surveyor under s.562), client obligations, fees, break clause, not-tax-advice, data protection, a 14-day cancellation right, confidentiality, liability capped at fees paid, entire agreement, governing law of England and Wales, and an execution block for both signatures. ### Why the automated control did not catch either, and what was done about it

 **`PASS_RE`**** matched only "N pass" and "N / 0 fail".** Neither `500 / 0 / 4` nor `862 passing assertions` contains either shape, so the drift checker read both files and reported nothing. **The sweep had already proved that day that the checker **_**can**_** fail — and it can, and it was still blind to the two most-quoted numbers in the project.** That is variant (vi) with a twist worth keeping: _a check that can fail can still be blind_, and proving it fails on a faked total tells you nothing about its coverage of real phrasings.

 Widened to catch the participle forms (`passing`, `passes`, `passed`) and the bare `N / 0 / N` triple. On the widened checker the Build Order line surfaced immediately as a present-tense failure. Both figures corrected; checker re-run **green**; negative control re-run and it now reports **8** failures where it reported 7. Backup at `.bak-phase95`. All three suites re-run afterwards, unchanged at 563 / 358 / 142.

### PHASE 95 — SECOND ADDENDUM: the prototype run was specified, 6 September 2026

 **Lakhbir's brief:** a working prototype to put in front of a developer — mock data, no live calls — plus a build spec so that when the developer receives the code they can see what is real and what they must build. Three surfaces: the existing site and assessment; a client portal; a Caprebate staff portal with a super user and four sections.

 **Three forks were put to him before anything was written, and all three were settled.**

1.  **The Accounting role is Caprebate's own finance.** It sees client name, claim value, fee, invoice and payment status — not the questions and answers, the register data or the surveyor's workings. **This is a change to the Developer Brief's actor table**, whose "Accountant (offline), no login" row describes the _client's_ accountant. That row stays true; the two must not be conflated, and Phases 103 and 107 both carry the correction.

2.  **Firing the research is one button.** Per-source status is displayed, which is the visibility he asked for, but the action fires everything outstanding — **which keeps the 4 September rule intact** rather than overriding it. An individual retry appears only on a call that actually failed, which is a different thing from choosing which sources to consult.

3.  **Block A is built first.** The engine is lifted out of the 758KB single file into a shared package before any surface is built, so the three surfaces compute from one estimate. Slower to a first demo by roughly a phase; the developer inherits a foundation rather than a mock.

 **Seven phases, 102 to 108**, written into the action plan and inserted before the sweep, with seven matching board items in FOR DEVELOPMENT. The sweep renumbered 101 → 109.

 **Two design constraints were made explicit in every phase, because a prototype is the most likely place to get them wrong.** The anchor quarantine is enforced **in the store, not in the screens** — a surveyor session must not _contain_ our estimate, and Phase 107 proves it by inspecting the payload rather than by looking at the screen, because a developer will copy whatever pattern they find. And **every mock is labelled as a mock on screen**: a convincing fake that is not in the handover table is the exact failure this exercise exists to prevent.

 **Three existing assets are reused rather than rebuilt, and one of them matters more than the rest.** The upload handler — 919 lines, 38 tests, twelve contract steps — **has never been called by anything**. Phase 104 is the first thing to call it, and demonstrating that is worth more to a developer than any screen in the run.

 **One structural fix, taken while renumbering.** The sweep's body no longer states its own number; it points at its heading. That is the defect this sweep found in its predecessor — heading 93, body 92 — and a number stated once cannot drift from itself. Renumbering is now a one-line edit.

### An API trap that cost three failed calls, and it is not the one in COORDINATES

 **`add_markdown_content`**** returns the ids of NESTED TABLE-CELL blocks mixed in with top-level ones, and the last id it returns is NOT the last block in document order.** Anchoring the next insert on that id fails with a bare `Internal server error` — including on a thirty-character payload, which is how it was diagnosed. The id in question was a cell inside a table earlier in the same payload, sitting at position 131072 alongside every other cell.

 **Two calls were wasted assuming it was a size limit**, because COORDINATES records that large markdown bodies fail. It was not size. **A one-line probe against the same anchor settled it in one call** — the negative control again, on a different kind of claim. Written into COORDINATES.

### The two questions the phase was told to answer, answered

 **Is the clawback in the letter? No.** Checked against all thirteen clauses rather than taken from the sweep. Clause 4 fixes the fee at 5% of allowances identified and never revisits it if that figure falls; clause 5 runs the other way and charges the client a break fee; clause 10 caps liability at fees paid, which reaches the same money only through litigation and is not an automatic credit. **Two live documents commit us to the mechanism** — the business plan recommends it, and the rules-defect plan states it as a rule, "not discretionary and not a goodwill gesture", because it is the control that removes our own financial interest in not reporting a defect we caused. Promising it in two internal documents while the contract is silent is itself worth a solicitor's view, and that is now question (e) on the register.

 **Is the parties-clause requirement met? Half.** The journey requires the letter to name who we contract with, who signs the filing position — the client's accountant if engaged, our own CTA disclosed and priced in if not — and that we do not decide what goes on the return. Clause 1 does the first, clause 2 assumes an accountant, clause 6 does the third. **The missing limb is the client with no accountant**, which is the limb the whole hybrid model turns on and the same assumption that breaks the s.203 notification handling.

No status was changed on any of the eight edited items, because in each case the label was already what was actually in the way.

 **API note worth keeping.** Three `add_markdown_content` calls failed with "This connector requires additional permissions" — an error that reads like an auth problem and is not one. A thirty-character probe against the same anchor succeeded immediately, and the payload went through unchanged once `docs(object_ids:[...])` and `->` arrows were removed from the body. **The error message names the wrong cause; treat it as a payload problem and probe the anchor before assuming size or permissions.**

 **NOT DONE.** _Nothing left as a sentence._ The wrong fee basis in six further documents is Phase 101, written and inserted before the sweep. The two clause gaps are board items with their evidence on them. The clawback's commercial terms are a question under Lakhbir's name. The stale "fee basis is an open decision" class in nine more documents is inside Phase 101's own prompt as class B.

## PHASE 92 — The brand debris the export could not reach

 _Run 7 September 2026 from a Mac, against the OneDrive copy of the tree rather than the Acer's. Five jobs, all closed. Two of the five turned out to rest on a premise that was no longer true, and finding that out was most of the work._

### The stale "blocked behind Q3" claim, in three data-protection documents

 **Fifteen edits across the three.** The brief described one table row in each. There were more, and they contradicted the documents they sat in: the breach and transparency pack has carried a Phase 57 amendment since 1 September saying the page is **no longer** blocked behind the name, while a channel table 950 lines further down still said it was. Corrected in each: the channel row, the paid-notice row, the social-profile row, the question row resting on the same premise, and a placeholder row reading "DOES NOT EXIST — blocked behind Q3" that both packs carried and neither Phase 57 nor the brief had noticed.

 **The distinction was held throughout.** What was corrected is the assertion that there is no channel and no available means. What was deliberately kept is that **the page is not built, because there is no website** — that is a build status and it is still true — and every ledgerstone.co.uk sentence, which records that a different trading business holds that domain.

 **The rights-request and complaints pack also carried a rename defect, and it was worse than stale.** Phase 88 had swapped a protected instance, leaving the document asserting that ledgerstone.co.uk redirects to a business "already using Caprebate". It does not; it uses the former name. That sentence was false rather than merely out of date, and it is fixed.

### Seven attachments, not six — and then an eighth

 The brief's heading said six and its list held seven. Seven is right. All seven were re-uploaded from disk under their Caprebate names onto the tax adviser's review pack and the rulebook-addendum item, and the old-named copies dropped. **One name in the brief was wrong**: the entitlement branch truth table is filed as `Caprebate-Entitlement-Branch-Truth-Table-B-v2.md`, with a `-B-` the brief omits; uploading under the brief's name would have misfiled it.

 **An eighth file carried the old name and appears in no list** — `12921255840__Ledgerstone-Statutory-Rules-Register.md`, the exported copy sitting beside the addendum on the same item, whose own contents Phase 88 had already corrected to read Caprebate. It is renamed on disk and re-uploaded. The tax adviser sees these filenames, which is the whole reason the job exists, and the eighth was as visible as the seven.

### The stale disk paths, and the two that were left

 **Fixed — four.** The backup and recovery policy, which said the working set is "currently held in" a folder that no longer exists; the developer handoff index, whose build-machine row also carried the note that the outer folder is misspelled, now untrue and deleted with it; the surveyor handoff index; and the consolidated back-end schema, which the brief left to judgement. That last one is a wayfinding pointer rather than a record, and it was **doubly stale** — it named both the old folder and the old OneDrive account.

 **Left, deliberately — two.** The OneDrive migration note and the shared file store are dated inventories. One compares two folders _by name_ and carries byte counts and checksums; the other opens by saying it was compiled on 27 August from a directory listing of that exact path. Rewriting either would falsify a record of what was on disk that day, which is the only thing it is for.

### The two jobs whose premise had expired

 **The removal mechanism works, and was used nine times.** It is how every old-named file on this phase's items was dropped.

 **The two mangled surveyor files were already gone.** The brief, inheriting it from the sweep of 6 September, said the item carried two unreadable files with good copies beside them under a `__CLEANED` suffix. It carries three files, no suffix, and both were downloaded and checksummed against disk: **byte-identical to the good copies.** Phase 88 fixed this and recorded that it had; the sweep carried the stale claim forward anyway, and it was in the brief a day later. Nothing needed doing and nothing was done.

### Also found and fixed

 **The rename broke a live cross-reference, and this phase caused it.** A document on the private hospitals question-flow item cited a rulebook by its old filename to evidence a verification. That citation pointed at nothing the moment the file was renamed, so it was corrected and re-uploaded in the same run.

 **The accountant's sign-off register had gone stale as a direct result of the work.** It told the accountant that seven attachments were still filed under the old name and were "queued for correction". They no longer are. That paragraph is rewritten, and it names the eighth file too. The surveyor register was checked and is accurate — it already records the damaged copies as removed. The solicitor, DPO and developer register mentions none of this.

### Re-derived at close

 **No suite was run, because nothing in this phase went near code.** Every uploaded asset was read back from the board and checked against disk: the two spot-checked in full are byte-identical, and every one of the nineteen matches on size.

 **No status was changed on any item touched.** Each label already said what was actually in the way — the two tax-adviser items await a signature, the surveyor and cyber-security items await Lakhbir, the valuation-database item waits on a licence, and the four data-protection records are finished instruments. Correcting a document's contents changed none of that, and inventing a status change would have been noise.

 **A correction to the removal mechanism as this document describes it.** The `name` field in a FileInput does **not** rename an existing asset. Passing an existing asset id with a different name is accepted, returns success, and silently keeps the old filename — tested here on the eighth file, which had to be re-uploaded to be renamed. `name` applies only to assets the call creates. The other half of the trap is confirmed as written: every asset is re-created on each call and its id changes, so the column must be read immediately before it is written.

 **The tree exists twice, in two different OneDrive accounts, and nothing said so.** This phase ran on a Mac, where the working copy is under `OneDrive - Aqlios LTD`, not the `OneDrive - IT Roadway` path the coordinates give. Both are complete; the Mac copy was verified at 880 files and current through Phase 95. **They are not one synced folder** — an edit in one does not appear in the other, and the board is the only thing the two machines share. That is now written into COORDINATES, with the rule that a phase writes its outputs back into whichever copy it read and then pushes the changed files to the board. Two traps went in with it: the junctions do not survive the sync, so the phase-suite folders under `03-app` are empty on the Mac and the suites must be run from `04-phase-work`; and the five hub documents are on neither disk, so a machine holding the tree but no Monday connector cannot read the plan it is meant to work from.

The sweep is renumbered to **Phase 110** so it stays highest and last.

## PHASE 96 — the £1m allowance cap, the two facts the engine read and never asked for, and the eleventh switch

 **Run 7 September 2026, on the Mac (Lakhbirs-MacBook-Pro.local), against the Aqlios copy of the tree.** Three board items, all three closed. Model: Opus.

### DONE — with the evidence

 **Job 1 — the £1m allowance cap, board item "Add a second test of the £1m allowance cap before the overheads fix ships". Now suite S in the site harness.**

 The premise needed correcting before the work started, and the correction is the useful part. The prompt said a grep for the cap returned zero and that there was no cap assertion in the harness at all. The grep was right; the conclusion was not. **One cap assertion already existed** — R11 asserts that the modelling module caps a first-year allowance at the statutory limit — but it reaches the limit through the rate table's symbol rather than the number, which is exactly why the grep found nothing. What genuinely did not exist was **any assertion at all on gate 2 of the cash-benefit gates**, the gate that decides whether a client is shown a cash figure, refused one, or told the question is open. Three branches, none covered.

 All three are now asserted, plus a fourth. "None left" closes the gate and withholds the figure, with a reason naming both the annual reset and the group. "Not sure" leaves it open — null, not false and not true. **Absent behaves identically to "not sure", asserted separately and word for word**, because absent is the state of every client who was never asked and a falsy test near that gate collapses it into a favourable answer while everything else goes on passing. A stated amount is the only branch that lets the figure stand. And the cap binds the money as well as the gate: a headroom above the limit still relieves only £1m in year one, spend exceeding the headroom takes only the headroom and the excess writes down rather than being lost, and an unknown headroom models no first-year relief at all rather than assuming the full £1m.

 **Job 2 — the two facts, board item "Ask the two questions the engine needs to model first-year tax relief".**

 The engine read the allowance headroom and the profit position and captured neither, so both arrived undefined on every real client — and not neutrally: an undefined headroom means no first-year relief is modelled (the slow end) while an undefined profit position means relief is taken in full every year (the optimistic end). Three questions now capture them, defined once in a shared module and spread into all five sector flows so the wording cannot drift, on the pattern the fixtures-history questions already set. "I don't know" is a first-class option on both choice questions, worded as an answer rather than a refusal, and it routes to the cautious branch — **never to 0 and never to £1m**. The amount is a follow-up shown only to a client who has just said they know it, because a money field cannot be skipped and would otherwise force a guess. A stated nil is recorded as "none", which is a third thing from zero and from unknown. An amount above £1m is flagged rather than silently trimmed, because a year's allowance cannot exceed the allowance — while the model still relieves no more than the statutory limit whatever is typed.

 **Job 3 — stamp duty, board item "Put stamp duty into the apportionable base — build the switch". The eleventh switch.**

 The switchboard held exactly ten and there was no eleventh. There is now, default false, both readings asserted per sector. When on, a shared module adds the transaction tax the client actually paid to the base, on the first line of the build-up in all five engines — ahead of the grant and contribution strips, so a grant-funded share of the price carries the tax paid on it out in the same proportion. It never computes or estimates a tax: no amount stated, nothing added, and the client is told so. It fires on a purchase and only on a purchase. **The name is resolved per nation** — SDLT in England and Northern Ireland, LTT in Wales, LBTT in Scotland — from the jurisdiction layer that already knew all four, asserted for each, including that a Scottish purchase is told about LBTT and never about SDLT.

 **The contradiction was written down rather than resolved**, in the switch's own comment, in the accountant register, on the board item and as a new question for the tax adviser: a competitor's real report puts the tax inside the base; our engine does not; and our own wording already tells every client outside England that acquisition costs ARE added. Whichever way the adviser answers, one of those has to change, and a close that does only its own half leaves the other half wrong.

### Four things this phase found that were not in its brief

 **The harness could not run on this machine, and it did not look like that.** `03-app/phase3` and `03-app/phase9` are NTFS junctions into `04-phase-work`, and OneDrive does not sync a junction — on the Mac copy both are empty folders. Five requires resolved to nothing, so Suites I, J and K reported the modules as **missing** rather than failing, which reads like a broken build and was really a broken link. The suite here reported 532 pass / 3 fail before the fix. The harness now traverses `03-app/<name>` and falls back to `../04-phase-work/<name>` when it is empty; on the Acer the junction is populated and nothing changes.

 **The new tests were negative-controlled rather than assumed, three ways.** Collapsing the absent branch of the allowance gate into the "unsure" test alone: three assertions failed. Flipping the eleventh switch on: thirteen failed. Making "I don't know" set zero: ten failed. A suite that cannot fail is worth nothing, and this one was made to fail on purpose before it was trusted.

 **The spread in COORDINATES did not sum, and the discrepancy was mine.** Counting a 200-id array by eye gave 203 Done against an items_count of 327, which looks exactly like the defect that block tells you to hunt. A second independent derivation — one `items_page` fetching status text per item, tallied in code — gave 204 and summed. **The lesson is now in COORDINATES: count them in code.** The board is at 327 items, up from 325; Phase 96 created none of them.

 **Two document-API traps cost work and are now written into COORDINATES.** Two inserts anchored to the same `after_block_id` land in reverse order — this put an ANSWER box above its own recommendation and had to be deleted and rebuilt. And an `add_markdown_content` payload arrived truncated at roughly 9KB, which is smaller than the 8-12KB the same block calls safe.

### NOT DONE — and where each one now lives

 **Whether legal and other incidental acquisition costs follow the transaction tax into the apportionable base.** The accountant register asks this as part 2 of its stamp-duty entry and only part 1 is built — nothing captures legal fees and nothing adds them. **It now lives as its own question in CAPREBATE QUESTIONS under the chartered tax adviser** ("When a building is bought, is the stamp duty part of the price we apportion?", which asks both halves in one answer block), and the register and the board item both say in terms which half is built and which is not.

 **Whether ****`aia_used_elsewhere`**** should be captured too.** Gate 4 reads it and no question sets it. It was deliberately left alone: the new allowance question already sets the headroom to "none" on the same facts, and setting both would print two near-identical reasons to a client for one fact. **It now lives as a note in the engine beside gate 4**, saying why it is uncaptured rather than leaving it looking forgotten.

 **Which of the two biases actually dominated a real client's figure.** Section 8 of the action plan asked which effect was larger. Both facts are captured now, but the answer needs real answers from real clients. **The section 8 entry has been rewritten to say so** — it is a reason to look again once there are live jobs, not an open build.

### Figures, re-derived and not inherited

|  Suite |  Before |  After |

|  `03-app/caprebate-regression.cjs` |  563 pass / 0 fail / 4 xfail |  **632 pass / 0 fail / 4 xfail** |

 Backups taken: `.bak-phase96` on the engine, the harness, and each of the five documents whose harness figure was corrected.

 **One more loose end, found at the close and given a home.** Phase 96 corrected the harness figure inside five documents on disk, and three of them also exist as **attachments on the developer handover pack item under two dead brand names** — Ledgerstone and Health Tax Partners. So those attachments are now not merely misnamed but **stale in the body**, which is a different job from the rename Phase 100 already owned. **Phase 100's job 2 has been rewritten in terms**: it now names the nine attachments on that item, says the fix is a re-upload from disk rather than a download-and-rename, tells the next phase to verify by grepping a downloaded copy for 563, and — because both lists in that prompt were found by query and neither was complete when written — gives it the one query that returns every asset on the board so it can derive the true count instead of trusting either list.

 **NOTHING LEFT** beyond what is named above. Every item this phase did not finish has a destination.

### Correction to this record, made the same day, after Lakhbir asked where the NOT DONE items actually live

 **The question was whether they were carried as a phase, and the honest answer was no — and worse than that, two of the four were not in any of the three permitted homes at all.** The carry-forward rule allows an existing later phase, a new numbered phase before the sweep, or a question in CAPREBATE QUESTIONS. The legal-fees half went to a question and the stale attachments went into Phase 100's job 2, which are both fine. The other two — the uncaptured "AIA used against other spending" fact and the unmeasured question of which bias dominated — went into **an engine comment and a paragraph of section 8 prose**, and this record claimed they were homed. They were not. "Prose is not a task" is the rule, and the first close broke it.

 **No new phase was warranted and none was created**, because neither is work Claude can do now: one is a decision that wants a second opinion, the other cannot start until there are live clients. What both needed was rule 7 — a board item. Both now have one, each with the reasoning written into an update rather than left in the code:

-  **"Decide whether the 'AIA used against other spending' fact needs its own question, or stays folded into the headroom one"** — Ready, Claude. It records why the fold was chosen (two gates would print the client two near-identical reasons for one fact) **and why that may still be wrong**: gate 4 is specifically AIA spent on OTHER expenditure, while gate 2 is no headroom for any reason, including a group company having used it — which is not the client's own spending at all. The item says in terms: do not simply set both from the same answer.

-  **"Measure which way the benefit figure actually moved once real clients answer the allowance and profit questions"** — Blocked, needs live jobs. It carries the one trap worth naming in advance: a client who answers "I don't know" is not the same as a client who was never asked, even though the engine treats them identically on purpose, so they have to be counted separately or the measurement concludes nothing changed for a group where nothing could change.

 **Board figures re-derived after those two items, and the spread sums:** 329 items — Done 204, Built-awaiting 51, Ready-Lakhbir 22, Ready-Claude 20, Blocked-question 11, Blocked-incorporation 9, Blocked-licence 8, Parked 2, Blocked-needs-live-jobs 2, Working-on-it 0. COORDINATES updated to match, and its spread instructions rewritten to prefer the single tallied call over ten filtered ones — which is what caused this phase's phantom one-item discrepancy in the first place.

## Phase 97 — A factor applied where its own source forbids it, and a "blocked" item that was not

 **7 September 2026 · Opus · Lakhbirs-MacBook-Pro.local**

### DONE

 **Job 1 — the location factor is no longer applied per element line.** The prompt asked whether the engine agreed with the specification. **It did not, and the defect was in both.** `residualApportionment` multiplied `loc.factor` into every element inside the costing loop, and the specification's worked example printed "Cardiff 94" in the source column of five element rows.

 **The finding that matters most: the arithmetic was never wrong.** One factor, uniform across every element, multiplies straight out of the sum, so `components.A` and `components.B` came to the identical figure either way. **No equality test on a total could ever have caught this**, which is why it survived. The tests written here assert the shape instead of the number.

 In the engine (`phase9/caprebate-cost-model.cjs`): element lines are now `qty × rate × depreciation × prelims × index` and nothing else, each carrying `location_adjusted: false` and **no ****`location_factor`**** field at all**, so a report generator cannot find one to print. The single factor is applied once to the summed total, **before** the fee band is looked up — the VOA fee scale is banded on construction cost, so applying it after would read the wrong band on any job near a band edge. `result.cost_plan` exposes the step. Two guards raise `E_LOCATION_FACTOR_NOT_APPLIED_ONCE`: every line must be explicable by the factors it declares, and the totals must be the line sum times one location factor and one fee factor.

 **The guard was proved, not asserted.** Test D10 rebuilds the module from source with the defect put back and checks it refuses. It was then verified in the other direction: disabling the per-line guard makes D10 fail, and only D10. It also asserts the mutant **passes with the gate off** — the honest reason this survived, since every shipped configuration is one the defect hides in.

 In the specification: the five element rows lost their "Cardiff 94" labels, and a new §10a shows the adjustment as the single step it is, with the gates shown off. **And the cause was found, which the board item had not named:** the design rule at "The rule that makes this work" _required_ the per-line adjustment and gave "Cardiff factor 94" as its model citation. Five rows were obeying the rule. Correcting only the rows would have left the defect specified.

 **The index base was left alone on purpose** and stays on "Adjust building costs for where the property is and how big the job is". Where the factor is applied and what it is indexed to are two different defects; only the first was independent of the £330 purchase.

 **Job 2(a) — the contract-size scale interpolates, and refuses off the ends.** It shipped as `bands: [floor, ceiling, factor]` read through `bandLookup`. Wrong twice: the published scale is a curve, not a step (a step makes two jobs £1 apart across an edge diverge materially, which the source does not say); and **the slot held a factor where the source publishes a percentage** — loading published figures straight in would have multiplied every cost by roughly minus five and still returned a number. Table shape is now `{ assumed_contract_value, quoted_as, valid_from, valid_to, points }`; `interpolateScale` and `percentageAdjustmentToFactor` are new and exported. **Out of range it throws rather than extrapolating** — and since the book's window is about £2m–£5m and the standing worked example is £6m, refusal is the path that fires first when the book is bought. `bandLookup` is unchanged and still used for the VOA fee scale, which genuinely is banded; test D16 asserts it still steps. Built against the empty table, gate still off: the mechanism ships, the data does not.

 **Job 2(b) — the free resolver was never checked, and it is available.** Re-verified that nothing resolves a property to a billing authority: `location_key` is an input the cost model consumes and **nothing produces**, which is the real reason LEG-E4 could not ship even with the book on the desk. The item had been recorded as VOA-licence-blocked. **The ONS route was checked today and works.** Office for National Statistics, Open Geography Portal; National Statistics Postcode Lookup (August 2026); **Open Government Licence v3.0, no negotiation and no fee**, subject to three attribution lines and a Northern Ireland carve-out that does not reach us because we serve England and Wales; `NSPL_AUG_2026.zip`, **176.5 MB** (185,109,467 bytes), CSV, no key or account; quarterly (Feb/May/Aug/Nov); 2,726,477 postcodes; field `LAD25CD`, which at England and Wales level **is** the billing authority for non-domestic rates. **Proved rather than assumed** — the ONS's own live service returned CF10 3NB → W06000015 (Cardiff), SW1A 1AA → E09000033 (Westminster), M1 1AE → E08000003 (Manchester).

 **Suites, all re-run after the changes:** site harness **632 pass / 0 fail / 4 xfail**; phase3 **358 / 0**; phase9 **142 → 151 / 0**; drift checker **green** — it went red first, on two lines asserting phase9 at 142 in the present tense, and both were corrected on disk. The Developer Brief's totals line was also **1,063 and behind its own A-block rows for the second time**; it is now 1,141 and carries a note saying to re-derive it rather than read it.

### NOT DONE

-  **The billing-authority resolver itself was not built.** It is a data-ingest job of its own, not a line in this phase. **New board item, "Resolve a property's postcode to its billing authority from the ONS postcode lookup", at Ready — Claude can build**, carrying the full research above including both build routes and the two things to get right.

-  **The specification claims a billing authority it cannot derive.** Its evidence table prints "Billing authority — Cardiff — _Derived_" and nothing derives it. **Named on that same new board item** as something to fix when the resolver is built.

-  **§7 and §10 of the specification state the same rebuild cost 9.6% apart** — £2,841,400 against £2,567,720 — and the 1.6% divergence the pack calls corroboration is computed off the smaller one; against §10 it is 8.9%. Not patched, because choosing between them is a valuation judgement. **New board item, "Two different rebuild costs for the same building", at Blocked — question, owner Surveyor; new entry S7 in FOR THE SURVEYOR; new question in CAPREBATE QUESTIONS under the chartered surveyor.** A caveat was added to §7 so nobody reads the 1.6% as settled meanwhile.

-  **The index base for the location factors** — "mean 100" against Spon's Outer London = 1.00 and a third base in the M&E book. **Stays on "Adjust building costs for where the property is and how big the job is", which was left at Blocked — licence or purchase**, correctly, with an update recording that its other half is now fixed.

-  **A pre-rename twin of the specification**, `Development/ledgerstone all/ledgerstone-full-specification-v8.html`, carries the same worked-example figures and the same uncorrected method error. Left alone because it is outside the Caprebate tree and nothing establishes whether it is a dead lineage or a second live fork. **Added in terms to Phase 100's prompt**, which is already sweeping pre-rename artefacts.

-  **The COORDINATES block still prints phase9 at 142 and the total at 1,132.** Corrected by a dated note directly beneath it, in the same convention Phases 92 and 94 used, rather than by retyping a 17.5 KB block that `update_block` can only replace whole. **Recorded here so it is a decision and not an omission.**

### Two things checked that turned out to be nothing

-  **`~/.Trash/Acer-work-files/Caprebate`**** is not a loss.** It holds 879 files against the live tree's 902, and exactly one file is present there and absent here — `12921255840__Ledgerstone-Statutory-Rules-Register.md`, which exists in the live tree under its post-rename name plus a `.bak-phase88` sibling. It is a pre-Phase-88 Acer snapshot, not a deleted working copy.

-  The prompt's claim that a grep for `billing_authority`, `location_key` and "council area" returns zero **was very nearly right but not exactly**: `location_key` does appear, 14 times, entirely as a parameter being consumed and asserted in tests. The conclusion — that nothing resolves a property to a billing authority — held.

## Phase 97 follow-on — the postcode resolver: built, and then run against the real file

 **8 September 2026 · Opus · Lakhbirs-MacBook-Pro.local**

 Phase 97 established that the free ONS route existed and put building it on the board. This is that build. It was asked for as "build what you can now, anything you can't add as a phase", and the split at the end is exactly that.

### DONE

 **The resolver exists.** `phase9/caprebate-postcode-authority.ts` (750 lines), `.test.ts` (**38 pass / 0 fail**), a streaming command-line ingest job, and a full specification. It resolves a UK postcode to its billing authority from an ingested ONS table and chains on to the price book's own regional key.

 **Two empty tables, and they are empty for different reasons — which the licence strings say in terms.** The postcode table waits on an ingest anybody could run this afternoon; the price-book key map waits on a £330 purchase. `resolveLocationKey` fails with a **different error code at each link**, so the message names which of the two is missing rather than reporting a generic failure. **A reader who conflated them would think buying the book was enough.**

 **The provenance layer gained a source it did not have.** `ONS_POSTCODE` under a new licence `ONS_POSTCODE_OGL` — **deliberately not the shared ****`OGL_V3`**** entry**, even though the licence instrument is the same, because ONS additionally requires an Ordnance Survey line and a Royal Mail line and the generic wording would under-attribute, which breaches the condition the licence is granted on. Four new tests hold that down.

 **The Northern Ireland carve-out is narrower than "Great Britain only", and that is commercial not pedantic.** Scotland is inside the grant; Northern Ireland is not. **Widening the business to Scotland is free and widening it to Northern Ireland costs a licence** — two decisions, not one. NI rows are dropped **at ingest**, so we never hold data we are not licensed to use commercially; the lookup refusal is belt and braces and is ordered _before_ the table read, so it cannot start silently succeeding the day a table is ingested.

### Then it was run on the real file, and that found three defects no test could

 The module was green at 30 assertions before this. **Every fixture was three lines long, and all three defects are invisible at three lines.**

1.  **Assumption A-1 was wrong, and the interesting part is that it moves.** The local-authority column is `lad26cd`, not the assumed `laua` — and it is **versioned by release year** (`laua`, then `LAD25CD`, then `lad26cd`). A hard-coded name does not merely fail today: it fails **every time ONS publishes**, which is quarterly, which is exactly the refresh cadence. It would have broken on roughly the fourth refresh and presented as a corrupt download. Now defaults to the verified name, falls back to the versioned pattern, and records `lad_column_used` so the table says what it was built from.

2.  **The module could not read the file it was written for.** The UK extract is **964 MB of CSV against Node's ~512 MB string limit**, so the only entry point threw `ERR_STRING_TOO_LONG` before parsing a row. Row logic is now incremental (`createNsplIngest`), the runner streams, and a test asserts the streaming core and the whole-file wrapper agree.

3.  **2,417 real postcodes were being called malformed** — historic Newport (`NPT`), which has a three-letter outward code. All are terminated so nothing would have resolved anyway; **what would have been wrong is the reason given to a client.** This module's own stated rule — a pattern that rejects a real postcode is a client who cannot be served, reported as _malformed_ rather than as our bug — was being broken by the module itself. `GIR` and `NPT` are now an explicit allow-list; `ZZZ 0AA` is still refused.

 **The proven run:** 2,729,091 lines read, **2,657,599 postcodes, 352 billing authorities, 0 malformed**, 63,293 Northern Ireland rows dropped. CF10 3NB → Cardiff, SW1A 1AA → Westminster, M1 1AE → Manchester, EH1 1YZ → City of Edinburgh, LS1 1UR → Leeds. BT refuses on licence grounds, NPT reports terminated, an unlisted postcode refuses rather than guessing.

 **A coverage limit recorded rather than smoothed over:** about **880 live GB postcodes (≈0.03%) carry no local-authority code** in this release. They are refused, not guessed.

 **Nothing large was left anywhere.** The download and the ~292 MB ingested table went to a scratch directory and were deleted; neither the repository nor the user's OneDrive holds them. The exact command that built it is §9 of the module's `.md`.

 **Suites, every one re-derived by running it:** site harness **632 / 0 / 4 xfail**, phase3 **358 → 362 / 0**, phase9 **151 → 189 / 0** across **four** files. Drift checker green — **it went red three times during this work and caught every stale figure**, including one I introduced myself. Total **1,183 passing assertions** (was 1,141).

### NOT DONE — and where each one now lives

-  **Nothing calls the resolver, and a 292 MB table has nowhere to live.** Deployment storage, wiring to the location factor, and the quarterly refresh duty. **New board item, "Make the postcode resolver actually run", at Ready — Claude can build, and written up in full as PHASE 110 in the action plan, inserted before the sweep.** Phase 102 does not cover it: that phase extracts the _site_ engine, and the phase9 modules are outside its scope.

-  **Whether the published-notice permission gate applies to this lookup at all.** It processes no personal data — the client's own postcode against a static public table, no external call, no third party. Our view is that it needs no gate; **that is a data protection judgement and not one to make in a code comment.** No second gate was built, per standing rule 13(b). **New question in CAPREBATE QUESTIONS under the data protection officer, with our recommendation and a worked example; new entry in FOR THE SOLICITOR, THE DPO AND THE DEVELOPER.** The module stays inert until it is answered, which costs nothing because the table ships empty.

-  **The map from council area to the price book's own regional key.** Genuinely blocked on the £330 purchase. **Stays on "Buy the Spon's price books" and "Adjust building costs for where the property is and how big the job is"**, the latter updated to record that its other half is now solved.

-  **`tableIsStale()`**** is built and nothing reads it.** Folded into Phase 110's job 3 in terms, rather than left as a function nobody calls.

 **NOTHING LEFT** beyond those four, each of which names where it now lives.

## Phase 98 — Four data-protection records that were specified and never written

 **8 September 2026 · Opus · Lakhbirs-MacBook-Pro.local**

 All four board items were at _Ready — Claude can build_ with **completely empty Files and Document columns**, re-verified at the start of this phase. Nothing had been produced for any of them.

### DONE

 **Job 1 — who we pass client data on to.** `Caprebate-Recipients-of-Client-Personal-Data-v1.md`, attached. Five recipients, seven processors, and whether anything has actually been disclosed to each (nothing has — no surveyor, no CTA, no live referral channel, no filed claim). **It found two contradictions between live documents:**

-  **Engagement Letter clause 7 says data goes "only with the surveyor and tax adviser".** The published privacy notice says we also share with the client's own accountant, which is a core part of the business model. **The two contradict each other and the client signs one of them.** And read literally clause 7 admits no processors at all, so it is breached the moment a client file is saved to OneDrive.

-  **The privacy notice lists sources as recipients** — "we share with... HM Land Registry, Companies House". We read from those; they receive nothing. The same section names **no processor at all**, while three of them hold client data today. This is precisely the source-versus-recipient merge the 30 August board note predicted a first pass would make. It had already been made, in the published document.

 **Job 2 — the four facts a breach decision turns on.** `Caprebate-Four-Facts-a-Breach-Decision-Turns-On-v1.md`, attached. The four facts were already specified; **the half that was missing is how we would establish each one inside 72 hours with what exists today. Three of the four cannot be, and two cannot be answered at all after the event** — device encryption has nothing recording its state before a laptop goes, and a first-ever restore test during a live incident is not a plan. The known limitation is restated, not designed around: **on the deputy route the two-person control is one person doing both**, and the DPO instrument is still unsigned.

 **Job 3 — suppliers' duty to tell us about a breach.** `Caprebate-Supplier-Breach-Notification-Duties-v1.md`, attached. Published terms read, not inferred. **Microsoft: 72 hours, to "administrators". monday.com, IONOS, AWS: "without undue delay", no period.** Two findings: **Microsoft's 72 hours is our entire Article 33(1) budget**, because our awareness of their breach _is_ their notification; and **the routing problem is worse than the deadline problem** — notifications land on an administrator address, not a monitored one, and an unread notification still starts our clock. **One outstanding check, two minutes and free:** IONOS's DPA has been automatic only since 19 July 2022; an older contract must complete it manually and is not covered until it does.

 **Job 4 — the Article 14 transparency record.** Built in `phase3/caprebate-name-exclusion.ts`, 17 new tests, phase3 **362 → 379**.

### The premise correction, and it is the second in three phases

 The prompt said `art14_notice_sent` appears nowhere in 04-phase-work. **That grep was correct. The conclusion drawn from it was not.** A full Article 14 transparency record **already existed** for the uploaded-document population — per-person notices, 14(5)(e) exemption reasons, a completeness assertion. Its own header even says that population was _"worse off than the register population because it has no store at all to add a field to"_, implying the register population had one. **It did not.** So the gap was real but narrower and better-shaped than described: the fix is a **mirror of an existing mechanism**, deriving the duty from the same name policy that permits the name, rather than a parallel invention.

 **What was added beyond the four specified fields is the part that makes them evidence.** Each field is plausible alone; the combinations are either evidence or nonsense. A notice sent on a date cannot sit beside a route of "no route"; NOTIFIED cannot be claimed when nothing was sent; **the 14(5)(e) exemption cannot be relied on for somebody we actually reached**, which is the single most likely way this gets filled in wrongly. A blank is refused on every required field and an explicit NOT SENT is accepted — exactly as the item asked. A corporate proprietor owes no duty, so the requirement does not fire for one. **Ingestion is deliberately not gated on it**, because Article 14(3)(a) gives a month and requiring the notice at ingestion would make lawful ingestion impossible.

 **Proved rather than asserted:** removing the exemption-versus-sent check fails exactly one test; making the duty predicate always false fails six.

### The question that did not exist

 Job 4's item has cited **"open question Q31"** since 29 August. **There was no Article 14 question anywhere in CAPREBATE QUESTIONS** — the document was restructured away from Q-numbers and this one was never rewritten. **This is the same failure the 5 September note describes**, where three items were blocked on a question nobody had drafted. It is now written up in full.

### Suites

 Site harness **632 / 0 / 4 xfail**, phase3 **362 → 379 / 0**, phase9 **189 / 0**, drift checker **green** — it went red once on the phase3 figure and was corrected in four documents. **1,200 passing assertions** (was 1,183).

### NOT DONE — and where each one lives

-  **The engagement letter and privacy notice amendments.** Findings, not fixes — amending a signed client instrument and a published notice is not Claude's to do. **New board item, "Clause 7 of the engagement letter forbids what the privacy notice promises", at Ready — Lakhbir action**, with the recommended clause wording.

-  **The four facts are still unknown.** The record of how we would find them out is complete; the facts are not. M1–M6 were **added as updates to the existing items that own them** rather than duplicated — the privacy mailbox item and the cyber security item — because both already existed and a fifth duty now waits on the mailbox.

-  **The four Lakhbir actions in job 3** — the IONOS check, the WordPress host contract, the surveyor's appointment terms, and nominating a data-protection contact. **The item is retagged Ready — Lakhbir action** and names exactly those four; everything published has been read.

-  **Whether the client route may be used for an Article 14 notice.** **New question in CAPREBATE QUESTIONS under the data protection officer.** The field was built either way; the answer decides whether that value may ever be used, and records carrying it are findable in one call.

-  **The identity standard for an E1/E2 subject.** Our proportionate rule authenticates nobody for this population. **New question in CAPREBATE QUESTIONS under the data protection officer.**

-  **Nothing logs, per data subject, which recipients actually received their data.** Article 19 is owed per record, not per firm, and a category list does not discharge it. Lands on the same systems decision as the Rules-Defect plan's "which clients are affected?" gap; **named in the recipients document §4 and not invented here.**

-  **Wiring the new assertion into a running system.** Nothing calls `assertArt14Complete` yet, exactly as nothing calls the document-population equivalent. **That is the prototype build's job**, and it is not a new gap introduced by this phase.

## Amendment 1 to the standing instruction, and the three orphans it was written for

 **8 September 2026 · Opus · Lakhbirs-MacBook-Pro.local · not a numbered phase — a direct instruction from the controller**

 **The instruction.** _"Each one of the phases should be checking if Claude did not build anything which it could have as it's not blocked — then this needs to be added to another phase. If something is blocked it needs to be added to the action plan or CAPREBATE QUESTIONS. This is the third time I had to ask."_

### The diagnosis, and it was a real hole rather than a lapse

 Every one of the thirteen live phase prompts was checked. **Twelve of thirteen carry rule 4's generic "give every loose end a home". Not one of them says how to decide WHICH home, and only the sweep ever looks at the board for work belonging to no phase.** The sweep runs last and occasionally, so between sweeps nothing catches it.

 **Three items proved it.** At the start of the session, three sat at _Ready — Claude can build_, covered by no phase, with no file and no document — checked by board id **and** by subject, because an item can be covered under a different name. Two engagement-letter defects found on 6 September, one allowance question found on 7 September. **All three were created by sweeps after the phase list was written**, which is the mechanism and will repeat every time a phase or sweep creates an item.

### The fix

 **STANDING INSTRUCTION, AMENDMENT 1** — a second block inside the standing instruction section, immediately before COORDINATES, adding **steps 4A and 4B**:

-  **4A classifies before routing.** One test: _could Claude build this today without anybody answering anything?_ **BUILDABLE goes in a phase** — not a board item on its own, not a sentence in a record, not a line in the chat, because a board item with no phase is how work sits still. **BLOCKED goes in a document** — a question under the person who must answer it, or a section of the action plan. "I ran out of room", "I did not think of it" and "it awaits a signature" are all BUILDABLE.

-  **4B looks at the board, not only at the phase's own scope.** Fetch every item at _Ready — Claude can build_, check each against the phase list by id and by subject, and give every orphan a phase before closing. One filtered call and one grep. **Do it even when the phase went perfectly — the orphans are never yours.**

-  **The closing check's NOT DONE list now carries a label on every line**: `BUILDABLE — <phase>` or `BLOCKED on <what> — <question or plan section>`. A destination without a label is a failed close, and so is BLOCKED for anything merely awaiting a signature or a purchase decision.

 **Deliberately not a fourteenth numbered point.** The document asserts "thirteen numbered points" in fifteen places; 4A and 4B extend rule 4 instead. **And deliberately a second block rather than a rewrite** — the standing instruction is 13KB, `update_block` replaces the whole of it, and hand-retyping the project's rules to insert three paragraphs is the one operation that can silently damage text nobody asked to touch. The section heading now reads "TWO BLOCKS: the thirteen points, then AMENDMENT 1. Both are the instruction."

### Then the rule was applied to its own three orphans — built, not parked

 **The clawback clause.** Now clause 13 of the engagement letter, _Fee Adjustment Where a Claim is Reduced_: the fee follows the corrected figure, credited or refunded, not discretionary and not a goodwill gesture — with the worked example in the clause, because the point of a percentage of a stated figure is that the client can do the arithmetic. **Three commercial terms left in square brackets** (trigger, settlements, time limit), matching the existing bracketed terms at clauses 4 and 5; the open question already asks exactly those three. Clause 4 now cross-refers to it and the execution clause has the client confirm they have read it. Execution renumbered 13 → 14.

 **The signatory of the filing position.** New paragraph in clause 1: where the client has an adviser, that person signs; **where they have none, a bracketed and switched-off route to Caprebate's own chartered tax adviser at a disclosed fee**; and where neither applies the client remains responsible — the case the letter previously left silent and the one a client with no accountant actually falls into today.

 **The AIA fold — confirmed, and it turned up a defect.** The second opinion reached a **stronger reason than the original**: as a boolean this fact cannot decide anything, because "some went elsewhere" does not establish that none is left, so a question capturing it would produce an answer that still could not size the relief. **And gate 4's reason was wrong**: it told the client "no headroom left for this spend" — in a case the harness already pins, with a headroom of £250,000 stated. Corrected without moving a figure; the gate still closes because that understates the benefit and is the safe direction. **Two assertions added** so neither the wording nor the fold can silently reverse, and the reversion was run to prove the first one fails.

### Verification

 Site harness **632 → 634 / 0 / 4 xfail**, phase3 **379 / 0**, phase9 **189 / 0**, drift checker **green** after correcting the figure in four documents. **1,202 passing assertions.** The engagement letter validates as well-formed with all 23 parts intact; backup at `.bak-phase98b`.

 **Rule 4B then run against itself:** the queue is now **12 items, every one covered by a phase (99, 100, 102–108, 110). Zero orphans.**

### NOT DONE

 **Nothing left.** The three orphans were built rather than routed, and the queue re-check is clean.

 **One thing named but not audited, and it is the obvious next place to look.** The amendment makes phases test the _Ready_ queue. **It does not re-test the eleven items at **_**Blocked — question**_** against rule 3**, which says something is only Blocked when building is genuinely impossible. Phase 97 found exactly that error once — an item parked behind a £330 purchase it did not depend on. **That is a sweep's job and the sweep already carries it**, so it has a home; it is recorded here because it is where the next buildable work is most likely hiding.

 **JOB 1 — the public notices page is built.** Four new files, all attached to the notices-page item and all written into `Development/Caprebate` on the Mac copy:

-  `03-app/caprebate-notices-page.html` — the page. Self-contained: no JavaScript, no external stylesheet, no web font, no image, because acceptance tests 6 and 7 require it to be readable with cookies declined and with scripts off, and the cheapest guarantee of both is a page that needs nothing it did not ship with. Every block carries a comment naming the document it was assembled from.

-  `03-app/caprebate-complaint-form.html` — the printable form, ruled lines rather than form fields, with a postal route and an email route. It exists because s.164A(2)'s "and by other means" is conjunctive.

-  `03-app/caprebate-notices-acceptance.cjs` — twenty-two structural checks, plus a `--live` mode that fails while any fact is unset.

-  `00-START-HERE/Caprebate-Notices-Page-Host-Checklist.md` — fourteen numbered lines with a verification step and a signature block, not prose.

 **The checks pass and they can fail — proved, not assumed.** Twenty-two pass. Stripping the objection block's border and injecting a `<script>` on purpose turned the run red on exactly the checks that should have caught it. **The first run failed four checks and three of those were defects in the checker, not in the page** — it read "nothing to sign up to on it" as a newsletter sign-up, counted a `rel=canonical` link as an external resource, and reported required passages as missing whenever they straddled a line break. All three are fixed, and the first one is worth remembering: **a check that punishes a page for describing its own compliance will, run often enough, get the sentence deleted.**

 **The fourth failure was real. Acceptance test 11 — the privacy notice must carry the full URL as text — failed.** The notice has been amended at v1.3: the URL is now in its own named block, written to survive a printout, with a plain "not live yet" line; Section 9's two square-bracket placeholders now carry real addresses; and placeholder 8, which blamed the missing page on the brand-name collision, has been corrected because that question was answered on 4 September. The amended file is on disk with a `.bak-phase99` sibling and has replaced the stale copy on the board.

 **JOB 2 — the two-tier rule is now in all three documents.** The premise was re-derived first and held: searches for the phrases it was recorded in returned **zero** across the developer brief, the build order and the provenance map. All three now carry the rule in full — free calls once the client is **informed** (not consented, with the reasoning), paid calls only after a server-side signature assertion and only on one operator click, every paid call running automatically on that click, no per-call confirmation, no second gate, nothing refusing and nothing throwing, and the status that nothing is firing today. **The provenance map's instruction to fire the title register "without thinking about it" is withdrawn**, and what survived of it — that no per-call budget approval is wanted — is now stated the way the rule states it.

## WHAT THE RULE BROKE, WHICH IS THE FINDING WORTH KEEPING

 **The address lookup is paid, and three documents assumed it fires in the pre-signature funnel.** The build order's **single most important acceptance test** read: a pass from S1 to S7 shows the address lookup and nothing else. That test and this rule cannot both hold. **The test is reversed** — a pass must now show no paid call at all — and the cost paragraphs that costed an abandoned funnel at one paid lookup went with it. The condensed front door survives, because the four registers it leans on are free and **the paid address ID buys match certainty, not access**: they are searched on a typed postcode and the paid lookup upgrades the match after signature.

 **The measurement that would set the confidence threshold has never been taken.** The matching specification says 200 properties. Every document now says so, and says do not assume it is good enough and do not assume it is not. **Nothing was decided about it here.**

## FINDINGS — five things that were not true when this phase started

1.  **The phase prompt's premise was wrong in a way that mattered.** It said no per-job cost model existed anywhere. `03-app/caprebate-business-plan-model.cjs` **does** compute cost per job, with a full sector cost table and a section headed "2. COST PER JOB". What did not exist was a **route**. The new module therefore restates that file's constants rather than inventing a second cost base, and Suite B parses it and fails if the two ever disagree.

2.  **The published cost tables could not be re-derived by running anything.** "Minimum fee — the research" (28 August) says its three-scenario figures came from re-running the business plan model "with the automation parameters changed" — and **that variation was never committed**. Suite F now regenerates all twenty-seven published cells from code and asserts them.

3.  **The published break-even purchase prices are stale by 2.5x to 4x, in our favour.** They were computed on 5% of **lifetime relief**; the basis changed on 3 September to 5% of **allowances identified**. The smallest dental job that pays for itself with a site visit falls from about **£798,000 to about £319,000** of purchase price. `reportsBasisChange()` computes it and test C6 pins it. **This paper should be added to the list Phase 101 is working through.**

4.  **The mutual-loss band exists, and it is not a small-job problem.** For a company client the fee exceeds year-one benefit at **every** level tested, up to £1.2m of allowances — so the band where we lose money _and_ the client is out of pocket runs from £0 to about £72,400 of allowances, but the client-poor half never ends. For unincorporated clients `CB_BENEFIT` returns **null** at every level, correctly refusing to guess without the pool split. **Closing the pool-split gap is what would settle it.**

5.  **Two claims in the corpus were false and are now corrected.** The ASA/CAP audit's **body** was not clean — 45 occurrences of the old brand, missed by the Phase 88 sweep. And the Phase 67 supersession record says the retired Client Journey (FINAL) "is not on disk" and that the only trace is a shortcut: **a 623 KB copy was attached to the developer handover pack the whole time.** It has been recovered to `_archive/superseded/` under a name that says it is retired.

Of its 45 occurrences, **33 are evidence** — audited file paths, a module identifier, and verbatim quoted site copy including the footer claim under audit, which literally said the old name on the date it was audited. Only the 12 entity references were changed; a note at the top of the document explains the convention so nobody "finishes" the rename.

## FINDINGS — four, and two of them were on neither list

 **1. The prompt said eleven documents. The true number is nineteen, and four of the extras are load-bearing.** A corpus-wide grep (not just the two lists) found the wrong basis asserted **as settled fact** in: the **Developer Build Order's Decided table** — the document whose entire job is to say what is decided — the **Developer Brief** in three places, the **full specification v8**, and the **monthly management accounts template** in two. The first two are attachments on the developer handover pack. All corrected and re-uploaded.

 **2. THE RATE CARD'S ARITHMETIC IS ON THE WRONG BASE, AND IT IS NOT A CORRECTION.** Asked to decide rather than assume, the answer is unambiguous. Its §1 defines the base twice: _"The fee is 5% of tax saved"_ glossed as _"'Tax saved' means total lifetime relief identified"_. **Lifetime relief is qualifying expenditure × marginal rate** — the fee-basis paper says so in terms — so every band, minimum, discount, uplift and floor beneath it scales a number **2.5× to 4× smaller than the one we actually charge on**. Fixing the headline sentence alone would have produced a document that reads as current and computes as wrong. **Banner added, sentence left standing, rebuild given a phase.**

 **3. The structural consequence is worse than the arithmetic one.** The rate card calls **claimant type** _"the largest single factor"_ and _"the first question asked"_, because a company at 25% produced 37% less relief than an unincorporated claimant at 40%. **On the decided base the client's tax rate does not enter our fee at all.** Claimant type stops being a fee-scaling factor entirely. Phase 100 had already proved this in code without connecting it to the rate card. **Five documents share this defect** — the rate card, the fee-basis options paper, the business plan's pricing sections, and both minimum-fee papers — because they all draw on one source.

 **4. The AML/KYC correction changes an argument, not just a word.** That paper's analysis leans on the fee being _contingent on relief recovered_ as evidence that the substance of the engagement is tax advice rather than valuation. **On the settled basis the fee does not depend on HMRC recovering anything.** The conclusion may survive; the reasoning has changed. Because the document goes to a solicitor it got a §0 correction notice saying so explicitly, rather than a silent word-swap — and the same correction **enlarges** its non-payment exposure, since the fee now falls due before HMRC has accepted anything.

## THE ANSWER TO THE QUESTION THE PHASE WAS ASKED TO DECIDE

 **The rate card's arithmetic is NOT on the right base.** It is on lifetime relief throughout — bands, per-sector minimums, portfolio discount, complexity uplifts and the 2.5% effective-rate floor. **It is a draft not in force and it must not go to Saddique in this state.** It has a do-not-quote banner and a rebuild phase.
