### The three findings, and two of them are about checks that looked fine

1.  **A green ****`tsc`**** does NOT prove N4 survives — this was tested, not assumed.** `AiaHeadroom` was collapsed to `number` on purpose and the whole-package typecheck **stayed green**, because nothing in the package's own TypeScript consumes the union in a way that would break. So the assertions were moved into `typetests/n4.types.ts`, and **proved able to fail first**: three separate breakages (collapsing the union, deleting `"unsure"` from `sufficient_profit`, removing `null` from a cash gate) each produced compile errors, and the restored file was clean.

2.  **Suite Q's yield-band drift trap cannot see the package.** It reads the bands out of the page text with a regular expression rather than out of the loaded module, so in `--package` mode it compares the _site's_ sector bands against the _package's_ shared table. Found by negative control: changing the care_homes purchase band in the package to `[0.20,0.55]` left the suite **green** at 634, and only the byte comparison caught it. **Deliberately not fixed here** — changing an assertion in the same phase as the extraction would have destroyed the before-and-after comparison the phase exists for.

3.  **Two recorded test commands do not do what they say.** `node --test 04-phase-work/phase9/` **does not run on Node 24** — the directory path resolves as a _module_, the run dies `MODULE_NOT_FOUND` and reports `1 test, 1 fail`, which reads exactly like a broken suite. A glob from the project root is worse: `*.test.*` also matches the `.bak-phaseNN` snapshots and silently runs them, producing thirteen failures that are not real. Corrected in the Build Order and Build-Prep-06 to `cd 04-phase-work/phase9 && node --test`.

 Also corrected in passing, all re-derived: the file index asserted **632** (the drift checker is blind to that line because its own text carries historical markers); the Build Order's §4 table said phase3 **358**, phase9 **142**, and "the **ten** CTA switches".

## PHASE 103 — The back end: real authentication, real roles, real authorisation (Block B). 8 September 2026

 **Board item:** BUILD 2 of 7 → **Done**. Machine: MacBookPro.localdomain, Mac copy of the tree. Built at `09-app/backend`.

### Nothing regressed, and the new work is tested

|  Suite |  Before |  After |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  `caprebate-regression.cjs` (site) |  634 / 0 / 4 |  **634 / 0 / 4** |
|  `caprebate-regression.cjs --package` |  634 / 0 / 4 |  **634 / 0 / 4** |
|  phase3 |  379 / 0 |  **379 / 0** |
|  phase9 |  245 / 0 |  **245 / 0** |
|  `09-app/backend` (new) |  — |  **81 / 0** |

 Drift checker green; its negative control reports ten present-tense failures, so it can still fail. Extraction verifier 21/21.

### DONE

-  **Node and TypeScript, strict, one process serving both applications.** `npm run typecheck` is 0 errors in `src/` and `test/` under `strict`, `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` and `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`. Clean checkout: `npm install`, `npm run migrate`, `npm run seed`, `npm start`, `npm run check`. **No hidden state** — database location, clock, hasher and transports are all passed to `buildApp`, so a test builds a whole application in memory and start-up does the same with different arguments.

-  **SQLite through ****`node:sqlite`**, built into Node 24, so a real database with real constraints and real migrations needs no server installed. Every table `STRICT`; foreign keys on; schema and migrations in version control.

-  **NO STRING-BUILT SQL, CHECKED RATHER THAN PROMISED.** `npm run lint:sql` fails on a template literal or a concatenated variable in a statement. **Proved able to fail.** It caught my own code first: `users.ts` was interpolating a trusted column-list constant, and that was rewritten rather than the rule being given an exception.

-  **`can(actor, action, object)`**, taking the specific object. **Deny by default is structural**: no rule for the action, no rule for the role, or a false predicate all reach one `return false`. A disabled user is refused before any rule can say yes.

-  **N1 enforced here, not later.** `src/payload.ts` asks `caprebate-anchor-quarantine.ts` rather than re-deciding, and builds the surveyor's object **from the released inputs forwards** — not build-then-strip, which is one forgotten key from leaking.

-  **argon2id** at the OWASP baseline behind a `PasswordHasher` interface; sessions server-side, httpOnly/secure/sameSite, rotated on privilege change with `rotated_from` recorded; **disabling a user revokes live sessions at once**; login and reset rate-limited; **generic failure messages**, and an unknown address still pays for a real argon2id verification so the timing does not answer the question either; reset tokens single-use, expiring, stored hashed, and consuming one revokes every session.

-  **Audit log append-only and tamper-evident, enforced twice** — `BEFORE UPDATE` / `BEFORE DELETE` triggers, plus a hash chain using the same scheme as the quarantine's own log (asserted equal on an actual hash, not merely described as similar). **No personal data in log lines, and the screen REFUSES rather than redacts.**

-  **Seed:** six invented businesses, all five sectors, six different stages, one user per role. **N2 wired in, not restated** — every register record goes through `assertNoUnauthorisedName`, so the seed cannot demonstrate a shape the real ingestion would reject. **No personal names at all**, which is stricter than N2 requires, because a developer reads the seed as the schema. `ZZ` postcodes. Seeding refuses without `CAPREBATE_ALLOW_SEED=1`.

-  **Three stubs, each one named module behind an interface:** email, register connectors, signature. Everything else real. Both gates recorded honestly as `NOT_PERMITTED_YET`, and **nothing refuses and nothing throws** when a gate is shut.

-  **Developer Brief actor table corrected** as the phase required: an **Accounting** row added for Caprebate's own finance, and the **Accountant (offline)** row reworded to say it is the CLIENT'S accountant, a different actor, still true, and not replaced by the new row. A note under the table sets out all three role vocabularies.

### Findings

1.  **A third role vocabulary was already in the tree, and conflating it was the trap the phase warned about.** `caprebate-anchor-quarantine.ts` declares its own five roles — `SURVEYOR`, `ANALYST`, `CLIENT_MANAGER`, `CTA`, `CLIENT` — written before the finance role existed. That module is the authority on N1 and was **not** rewritten. `src/roles.ts` holds the single mapping, under test. **Accounting has no counterpart there at all**; it maps to a non-quarantined staff role, because the quarantine's only question is "is this the surveyor".

2.  **The role test found a real authorisation bug in the first version of the rule table.** `business.read` for a CLIENT used a predicate reading `o.business_id`, but a _business_ object's own id is `id` — it has no `business_id`. The predicate returned `undefined === <id>`, so **every client was refused their own record**, and a rule that refuses everything looks exactly like a rule that is working. Fixed, and the reason is written beside it, because that failure mode returns whenever a new object type joins the union.

3.  **The password-leak test could have proved nothing, so it was made able to fail.** It searches responses and audit rows for the plaintext — but only detects a leak if the fixture's stored value contains the plaintext. The test hasher deliberately stores `fake$<password>`, and **a separate assertion proves that**, so the leak checks cannot pass vacuously against a hasher that never had the password in it.

4.  **Three type errors exist in ****`caprebate-anchor-quarantine.ts`**** and none is a defect.** All three are `arr.length ? arr[arr.length - 1].x : fallback` — correct, guarded code that `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` cannot narrow. Those files have **never been type-checked**: until Phase 102 there was no compiler in this project at all, and Node runs `.ts` by stripping types without checking them. `tools/typecheck.cjs` fails the build only on this package's own diagnostics and **prints the external ones every run rather than hiding them**.

### NOT DONE

 **NOTHING LEFT.** Every requirement in the phase prompt is built and tested, and the scope beyond it belongs to phases that already exist: the screens are Phases 104–107, and the domain tables this phase created carry no behaviour of their own — they exist because an authorisation layer tested only against invented shapes proves nothing about the application.

### Checked and found clean

-  **Orphan check (Amendment 1, step 4B).** All ten items at `Ready - Claude can build` matched to live phases by id and subject: BUILD 3–7 are Phases 104–108, attachments is Phase 111, the postcode resolver is Phase 110, the two fee items are Phase 112. **No orphans.** The two fee items still sit in group Z while carrying a live status — correctly tagged, correctly owned by Phase 112; it is the group that is wrong, and it was flagged the same way by Phase 102.

-  **Sign-off registers:** no change. Block B is code proved by tests, so the item went to **Done** rather than `Built - awaiting sign-off`, and nothing new awaits the accountant, the surveyor or the solicitor/DPO/developer. The Developer Brief edit is a correction to an existing document, not a new item for signature.

A second instance in the same paragraph — a placeholder reading `[link — public data protection page; blocked on Q3]` — was not visible to the prompt's own grep terms.

3.  **The prompt said the response letters carried three hits. They carried six**, and one of the six is the row that sends a reader to the interim-step board item, which is exactly the row a person acts on.

4.  **`update_assets_on_item`**** really does re-create every asset id, and it was watched doing it twice in one run.** The id returned by `finalize_asset_upload` is not the id the column holds a second later. **Read the column immediately before the write and never reuse an id from earlier in the same run** — COORDINATES says this and it is exactly right. Also: the mutation takes `board_id` / `item_id` / `column_id` and `files:[{assetId, fileType, name}]`, and **`fileType`**** is the lowercase enum ****`asset`****; ****`ASSET`**** is rejected.**

### NOT DONE

It has cleared — is that review due now?"** The wording was deliberately left as it stands: correcting a blocker attribution is one thing, re-pointing a review trigger at a later event is another, and doing the second would quietly cancel a review the condition has already called for. **That is the only thing this phase found and did not fix.**

# PHASE 104 — Caprebate HTML: the site, the assessment, the login and the client portal

 **8 September 2026. Opus, on the Mac copy of the tree. Block C of the Developer Build Order — deliverable 1, finished in one phase.** Everything lives in `09-app/backend/src/web/`, mounted ahead of the JSON API in `src/server.ts`: **one process, one session store, one ****`can()`**.

### DONE

-  **The opening move works end to end, over real HTTP.** Six screens → the engine's figure → the funnel close → a `businesses` row, an `assessments` row, **one ****`assessment_answers`**** row per question** and a `bookings` row the back end can see. Walked with a care home at £1.85m: the engine returned £740,000 and the twelve answer rows came back with `Q1a` as **DONT_KNOW**, not as a blank.

-  **The client-facing copy, the question wording and the order were PORTED, not improved.** Every string in `SCREENS`, `OPTIONS` and `COSMETIC_NOTE` is transcribed from the site's own renderer (`FN.screenQ1` … `FN.screenQ3`). A test asserts `SCREEN_IDS` equals `CB_FUNNEL.SCREENS` exactly, so the order cannot drift.

-  **It calls the engine PACKAGE.** `src/web/engine.ts` is the only file that imports it — one line to grep — and every gate, band, channel, figure and assumption comes from there. Nothing in the web half decides a tax question.

-  **The login is Phase 103's, unchanged.** Generic failure messages, rate limited, server-side sessions. **A client reaches only their own record**, and the test that proves it is the first one in the file.

-  **All five portal sections.** Progress in the client's own words; the engagement letter rendered from the .docx with its open terms shown blank; the appointment read from the same `bookings` row the staff calendar will read; the questions-we-still-need-answered list, where an answer records **who gave it**; and documents.

-  **THE UPLOAD HANDLER RAN, UNMODIFIED.** See the findings.

-  **Archived, not deleted:** the journey wireframe, the client script, the business flow and the supersession note, to `_archive/superseded/` with `README-phase104-supersession.md` saying where each one's content went.

### Findings

1.  **BLOCK A HAD NEVER BEEN LOADED BY ANYTHING, AND COULD NOT BE.** `09-app/engine/src/index.ts` used `import x = require(…)`, which Node refuses outright in type-stripping mode — `ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX`. Phase 102 type-checked it and verified the extraction byte-for-byte, but **nothing had ever imported it at runtime**, which is precisely the defect it was built to fix in the site file. Phase 104 is the first caller. Fixed with **default imports**, which work under both `tsc` and Node; `src/generated/` was not touched and `verify-extraction` is still 21/0.

2.  **THE UPLOAD HANDLER RAN FOR THE FIRST TIME SINCE 31 AUGUST, AND IT RAN UNMODIFIED.** 945 lines, 38 tests, no consumer. It now discharges **steps 1 to 7 of the receipt contract** against a real `ObjectStore`: classify, segment, **strip**, write, **delete the unredacted original with evidence**. Under `FAIL_CLOSED_SETTINGS` the raw file is never promoted, and a test asserts `raw_file_promoted: false` and that the quarantine key is no longer readable. **`assertContractCovered()`**** is green and is called on the request path, not only at start-up.** Proof it was not edited: nothing in `04-phase-work/phase3/` has a modification date later than 08:46 on 8 September, there is no `.bak-phase104` in that folder, and its own suite is 379/0.

3.  **MIGRATION 002 HAD INVENTED A SECOND BOOKING VOCABULARY, AND IT RE-ADMITTED VIDEO.** `bookings.channel` allowed only `telephone` and `virtual`. CB_BOOKING's channels are `phone`, `sms_whatsapp` and `email` — and `virtual` **is** the video channel that Phases 69–71 deliberately removed on 3 September, whose own comment says "Do not quietly re-add it here". A CHECK constraint that accepted nothing else would have re-added it by making everything else unstorable. Rebuilt in migration 003 onto CB_BOOKING's three, with `CHECK`s that only `phone` may carry a time. **The phase prompt's own "four channels" was wrong for the same reason** — four is `businesses.preferred_contact`, a different column and a fourth vocabulary again.

4.  **THE HANDOVER PACK'S FILE READS WERE BY ARRAY INDEX.** Archiving the journey wireframe broke suite M4; adding the application that replaced it then broke **M5**, because `HANDOVER[5]` had silently become a different document. Both now look up **by name**, and the comment records why. The wireframe stays in the pack at its archived path — it is still the only record of the screen sequence as first drawn.

5.  **The engagement letter has EIGHT unresolved terms, not three**, and they are derived from the document rather than listed — clause 4's fee basis, payment terms and abort fee; clause 5's break fee; clause 13's trigger, settlements and time limit; and one in clause 1. It also carries a **specimen client name and a specimen range**; the name is substituted and the range is flagged, because rendering a template unchanged would show a client somebody else's name in their own contract. The letter has **fourteen** numbered clauses; the prompt said thirteen.

6.  **The .docx zip really does use a backslash entry path.** `word/document.xml` returns "filename not matched" — the trap COORDINATES warns about, walked into within the hour. The reader tries both spellings, and it was rewritten to use `node:zlib` rather than shelling out to `unzip`, which is not on a stock Windows machine.

### Requirement W1 — which acceptance tests pass, and which does not

|  Test |  Result |
| --- | --- |
|  **W1-T1** |  **PASSES.** No path returns a document or a listing, and a source-level assertion proves the router has no static file route at all — with a negative control so the assertion is known to be able to fail |
|  **W1-T2** |  **PASSES.** Logged in as another client, the download returns 403 |
|  **W1-T3** |  **PASSES**, and the test is the strong form: a document is moved to another business mid-session and **the very next request is refused**. A capability cached at session start would let it through |
|  **W1-T4** |  **NOT RUN — NEEDS THE REAL HOST.** It is about the WordPress Media Library, REST API and sitemap, and there is no WordPress in this build. Declared in the test file and deliberately NOT counted as a pass |
|  **W1-T5** |  **PASSES.** Files `0600` (no execute bit for anyone), directory `0700` (nothing for group or other), a PHP payload named `.pdf` refused on server-side sniffing, the size cap enforced, and write capabilities scoped to a single key |
|  **W1-T6** |  **PASSES.** Every serve writes an access record naming who, what and when — **including the refusals** |

 **One thing the download endpoint does that is worth stating plainly: it returns 410, not bytes.** Under fail-closed settings the original is deleted once the strip has run and is never promoted, so **there is nothing to serve**. Inventing a copy to serve would undo the control the pipeline exists to perform.

Already covered — the developer handover pack (item 12937209644) carries W1 and its six tests, and Phase 108 folds the acceptance list into the Developer Spec. **No new question is needed and none was invented.**

A fake that invented plausible PDF text would be worse than useless: the strip would then be stripping content nobody uploaded. It is one named module behind the port, so replacing it is a swap.

# PHASE 105 — the back end: settings, filled assessments and the calendar

 **8 September 2026. Board item 12984660318 (BUILD 4 of 7). Block D of the Developer Build Order.** Settings first, because working times are the booking system's only input and the calendar cannot be right until they exist.

## DONE — what this phase actually completed, with the evidence

### Settings, and the test the brief singled out

 Per user: **password change, username, display name, profile photograph and working times.** ADMIN only: **create a user, assign a role, disable a user.**

 **The brief asked for proof that the four non-admin roles cannot reach any of it — "not that the menu is hidden, that the ENDPOINT refuses".** Every administration test is a real HTTP request on a real session cookie against the real server, for every role, driven from `APP_ROLES` rather than from a list typed in the test — and each asserts a 403 **and that nothing changed**, because a 403 that still wrote the row would pass a status-code assertion and be exactly the defect worth catching.

 **A disabled user's sessions end immediately**, asserted through the same cookie on the very next request. A **role change** revokes them too: a demoted user keeping the permissions they were just relieved of for eight hours is the same defect wearing a different name.

 **Admin power is over an account, not inside it.** `user.change_own_profile` and `user.set_photo` are `self` for **every** role, ADMIN included. An administrator can create, re-role and disable; they cannot change somebody's name, username or face, because a record edited that way reads as the person themselves. There is a test that an administrator's own post changes only the administrator.

### The profile photograph, down the same hardened path as a client document

 `src/web/images.ts` is a dependency-free PNG decoder and encoder, and it exists because **a magic-number sniff protects nothing**: every attack that matters lives after the first four bytes — a payload in a `tEXt` chunk, bytes appended after `IEND`, a polyglot a second parser will run.

 **So nothing the client sent is stored.** The bytes are decoded to pixels and a **new** file is written from those pixels. What survives is the picture; everything else is gone by construction rather than by being stripped, which means there is no list of things to remove and therefore no list to get out of date. Tests build real files carrying real payloads and assert the payloads are not in what we keep, and that the picture is byte-identical either way.

 **PNG alone, and that is a decision rather than a shortfall.** A real re-encode needs a real decoder; JPEG needs a DCT decoder and this package has one runtime dependency on purpose. The alternative — accept a JPEG and store it unchanged — is the thing the file exists to refuse. A JPEG is refused **by name, saying why**.

 **Decompression bombs are refused from IHDR before any inflate**, and the inflate is capped at the byte count those dimensions imply. Both, because either alone leaves the other open. Files `0600` in a directory `0700` outside the web root; served only through an endpoint that authorises the request; the object key is a hash of the user id, so a listing of the store is not also a list of who has an account.

 `src/web/multipart.ts` is a deliberately ungenerous reader, because the pages work with JavaScript disabled and a browser form carrying a file has one encoding. Seventeen tests, mostly of refusals.

### Section 1 — filled assessments

 Newest first, with the business, sector, property, range shown, submission time and **the contact method that decides what happens next**. Opening one shows **every question in the order asked**, with skipped questions shown as skipped and "I don't know" shown as an answer — there is no code path that renders an empty answer cell, and the test asserts that on the rendered table rather than on the labels.

 **A distinction the fixture now establishes and the schema already kept:** a question that was ASKED and left blank is `SKIPPED`; a question the funnel never reached produces **no row at all**. "Nobody asked" and "asked, not answered" are different facts about a claim.

### The client's number and the staff's number cannot differ

 The brief: _"If the staff view and the client view of the same number ever differ, that is a defect, and a test should assert they do not."_

 **The defect it was guarding against was rounding, not wording.** `assessments` stores integer pence; the funnel computes in pounds as a float. Rounding the float for the client and the pence for the back office agrees _almost_ always — £1,234.4999 becomes £1,234 for one and £1,235 for the other — and "almost always" is the worst property a quoted figure can have. `src/web/shown-range.ts` converts **once**, and four screens render the same function of the same integer. The test drives the funnel over HTTP, scrapes the figure the client was shown, and asserts the same string appears on both staff screens.

### N1 reaches these screens

 `range` is **added** where `estimate.read` passes, never removed where it does not — built forwards, the way `src/payload.ts` builds the surveyor's object. A SURVEYING actor reads the assessment inputs and the test looks for the estimate three ways: the rendered figure, the raw pence at any depth of the response, and the figure in whole pounds. ACCOUNTING reaches neither section.

### Section 2 — the calendar

 Day and week views, who it is assigned to, and the channel. **Bookable slots come from working times — one function, and the staff calendar, the staff booking page and the client's own funnel-close picker all ask it.** The write path asks it **again** at the moment of writing, so a time that never appeared on any screen is refused: the picker is a courtesy, the refusal is the control.

 **A booking made in the client's journey appears without anybody re-entering it**, and the brief's demonstration is a test: schedule one, assert the client's portal shows it; move it, assert the portal follows and the old time is gone; assert there is still **one** row and that `booking_changes` holds both moves.

 **The client can now pick their own moment at the funnel close**, from the same slot function — with the people taken out, because a visitor who has given us no name should learn that Tuesday at ten is free and not whose diary it is.

## THREE DEFECTS FOUND BY OPENING THE SCREENS, NOT BY REASONING ABOUT THEM

 Each is now pinned by a test. They are recorded together because the lesson is the same one: the tests were green before each of them was found.

1.  **"Every slot is already taken" for a day whose hours had simply passed.** Nothing was booked at all. A staff member would have gone hunting for bookings that did not exist. There are now **four** unavailability states, not three, and `WINDOW_PASSED` is separated from `FULLY_BOOKED` by asking the same question with and without the "not in the past" floor.

2.  **An unassigned booking was auto-assigned to whoever's hours covered the slot** — which, on the seeded data, was the **finance** user. Setting working times and being bookable were the same permission and are not the same thing. `bookableUserIds` now asks `can(..., 'booking.write', ...)` rather than carrying a list of role names.

3.  **The booking picker offered the same moment once per free diary.** 09:30 and 10:00 appeared twice each. `distinctMoments` collapses them for a picker and leaves the per-diary list for the assign control.

## A FOURTH CONTACT VOCABULARY, RETIRED — and the first attempt was wrong

 Migration 002 allowed `preferred_contact IN ('email','telephone','virtual','post')`. CB_BOOKING's channels are `phone`, `sms_whatsapp`, `email`. **`'virtual'`**** is VIDEO, deliberately removed on 3 September 2026, and ****`'post'`**** was never a channel — and both were in the seed**, so a staff screen showing "how did they ask to be contacted" would have displayed a channel no client can pick, and a developer reading the seed as the schema would have rebuilt video. `src/web/assessment.ts` already had a comment calling it "a FOURTH vocabulary" and quietly mapped between the two, which is what kept both alive.

 **The plan was to narrow the column with triggers. It cannot be done** — a trigger can only make a column stricter, and `phone` is not in 002's CHECK. The seed failed on the first run and named the constraint. Rebuilding the table is the documented fix and **thirteen tables carry a foreign key into ****`businesses`**, so the column was **ended** instead: every value set to NULL, two triggers refusing any value at all. The channel lives on the booking row, in CB_BOOKING's words, and that is now the only place it lives. Physically removing the column is Job 3 of Phase 113a.

## TWO THINGS THAT WERE NOT ASKED FOR AND WERE BUILT ANYWAY, BECAUSE THEY WERE GAPS

 **A client had nowhere to change their own password.** `handleSettings` is mounted twice — `/staff/settings` and `/portal/settings` — as **one implementation**, so a password change cannot rotate the session on one and forget on the other. What differs is the shell and which sections are drawn; every authorisation is the same `can()` call, and a client posting to the working-times route is refused by the rule, not by the absence of a form. There is a test for exactly that.

 **`/staff/settings`**** was reachable by a CLIENT** until this was noticed: `user.read_self` is `self` for every role, so the page rendered perfectly well for somebody with no business in the back office. `backoffice.enter` is now a rule in the table, asked once for the whole `/staff` prefix, and every section still authorises its own objects behind it.

 **`assertNoStaticFileRoute`**** now reads every file in ****`src/web/`****, not only the router.** It was right while the router was the only thing that could answer a request; `staff.ts` serves the photograph. Widening it made it fail on `objectstore.ts` itself, because the bare `/serve-static/` pattern matched the literal in its own list — so the two library patterns now require an import context, and no file is excluded. Five negative controls, one per pattern.

## And one correction to Phase 105, found by running its suite

 **A test asserting a refusal message had a hard-coded date that expired on 9 September.** `staff.test.ts` posted `2026-09-09T03:00:00.000Z` expecting "outside the working hours" and got "that time is in the past": the application uses the real clock and that moment had become the past. **The refusal still worked — it was refusing for the wrong reason**, and the assertion on the message is what caught it. The time is now computed from the clock, so it is always in the future and always outside a working day.

# PHASE 107a — three things Phase 107 found and deliberately did not fix

 **9 September 2026. Board item 13004035199. Machine: Mac.** Two corrections to earlier work, one reconciliation, and one job left on purpose.

## DONE — what this phase completed, with the evidence

### JOB 1 — all 31 questions in the archived brief are reconciled, one by one

 **The premise was re-derived first, and one part of it was wrong.** The phase prompt describes the brief without dating it. **It is version 0.1, prepared 21 June 2026** — the oldest live document this project had, written roughly a hundred phases before the reconciliation. That single fact reframed the job: this was not a check that 31 questions had homes, it was a check on whether **31 ten-week-old assumptions were still true**. Several were not.

 **The output is a 31-row table in ****`_archive/superseded/README-phase107-supersession.md`**, one row per question, each naming where it now lives AND whether its assumption has been overtaken.

 **Four assumptions had been reversed or dissolved, and these are the ones worth knowing:**

-  **A1** — the brief says a care home's SBA position is _"treated as contested… we flag for sign-off, never assert"_. **Rulebook E now makes a positive finding with a statutory cite** (row E-E5, the s.270CF(1)(a)(v) personal-care exception): SBA is available. The residual is narrower and better — review-pack subitem E-Q5.

-  **A3** — the brief asserts AIA is allocated to the special-rate pool first. **The engine no longer asserts it.** Where the allocation is unstated it models **both orderings and returns a range**, naming Rulebook I question I-Q5 as the reason. An assumption became a declared unknown.

-  **A10** — **the mechanism the question is about no longer exists.** The Stage-3 conditioning rules (upper/lower half of the band, a 15% pre-2008 integral-features uplift) were removed when Phase 72 replaced the sector-picker flow with the condensed front door. `CB_BAND.rangeFor` returns the plain band. The question could not be answered as posed.

-  **A14** — the brief recommends a fee _"quoted against recovered tax benefit"_ and warns against _"a percentage of allowances identified"_. **Lakhbir settled the opposite on 3 September 2026 (Q55).** The recommendation was rejected on the merits.

 **FOUR OF THE 31 HAD NO HOME AT ALL.** Three questions were written to give them one, all in CAPREBATE QUESTIONS, in the six-part shape with an answer block:

-  **"Are our five sector percentages anywhere near right?"** (surveyor) — this is the one that matters. `CB_BAND` still holds exactly the brief's June bands; the module's own comment calls them _"assessed bands — Caprebate's own reading … not independently calibrated"_; they produce **the only number a client ever sees**; and nobody was being asked to validate them. **A10 folded into it**, because the residual concern outlived its mechanism.

-  **"What counts as too far apart when we test ourselves against a real claim?"** (surveyor and tax adviser) — the golden-case tolerances, plus the fact that **the anchor may be circular**: the flat 15% professional-fees figure has no cited source and our own cost-model notes record it _may have been back-solved to reproduce that very case_. **C1's sign-off routing folded into it.**

-  **"Has anybody actually checked that we are allowed to be called Caprebate?"** (Lakhbir) — **deciding a name and clearing a name are two different jobs and only the first has happened.** The brand note's own six-step sequence has step 2 as _"run a UK trade mark search on the chosen name"_; steps 1 and 3–6 are done and **step 2 alone was skipped.** That note is also written about **Ledgerstone** and closes by asking whether the trade-mark question should be its own board item, observing _"it is a real risk that this note surfaces and does not close"_. It did not close.

 **One rename scar recorded rather than left to confuse.** The brief's C8 reads _"raised … against the former working name 'Caprebate'"_, which is nonsense on its face. The Phase 73 corpus rename replaced both occurrences of the old name — including the one that existed to name the old name. It should read _Ledgerstone_.

### JOB 2 — `caprebate-surveyor-crm.ts` gained `NOTHING_PROPOSED`

 **What every metric does with it was worked out BEFORE it was added**, which the prompt required and which turned out to be the whole safety argument: `adoption`, `selfConsistency`, `drift`, `divergences` and the blank-field control **all exclude it by construction**, because every one of them filters _positively_ on `CALIBRATION_ORIGIN` or `SURVEYOR_LIBRARY`. **No metric needed a new clause.** That reasoning is written into the module beside the value.

 **One deliberate addition beyond the minimum.** `adoption` now reports **`excluded_nothing_proposed`** on its own line rather than folding it into `excluded_not_platform_default` — _"they used a different source"_ and _"we offered nothing"_ are different facts about the capture flow, and merging them would hide which one we are looking at. It matters here: a high count on that line means **we are not putting our own figures in front of the surveyor at all**, which is Caprebate's actual state.

 **The Phase 107 fallback in ****`09-app/backend/src/web/surveyor.ts`**** is deleted**, and the call site is `propose` again with nothing wrapped round it.

 **A defect the suite caught mid-change, and it is the most instructive thing here.** `libraryFor` in the back end **restated** the module's guard instead of asking it. When the module's guard widened, the application went on dropping exactly the events the module had just learned — so the library still looked empty and the fix looked like it had failed. **A mirrored rule is a rule with two homes**; the comment there now says so, and says that this is the second time it has mattered.

### Also corrected, under step 2 — a document that did not know its own item was closed

 `04-phase-work/phase9/calibration-instrument-v1.md` listed **O-1**, _"the positive-confirmation step in the surveyor's flow — the type exists; the capture does not"_, as open. **Phase 107 built it**: the workspace puts an _"I looked at this field"_ box against all ten tracked rate fields. Closed, with the reason, and the _"remaining work (O-1, O-2)"_ sentence corrected to O-2 alone.

### A new writing trap, recorded in the action plan

 **The last block id ****`add_markdown_content`**** returns is not necessarily a valid anchor.** Where the markdown contained a table, the returned ids include the table's **cell children**, which sort last; anchoring the next insert on one fails with an opaque _"Internal server error"_. **It looks exactly like the payload-size trap already recorded** — which is what made it cost twice: splitting a 5 KB payload to 1.8 KB failed identically, which is the evidence that size was never the cause. Both failures wrote nothing, verified by re-reading before retrying.

### WRITING §4 FOUND A FOURTH STUB, AND THAT IS THE POINT OF §4

 **`plainTextExtractor`**** in ****`src/web/uploads.ts:72`**** opens with the words **_**"and it is a STUB, declared as one"**_** — and it was in no list.** `STUBS` in `src/app.ts` said _"THE THREE STUBS… so that what is not real here is a question with an answer rather than a search"_, and a test asserted exactly three. **A stub that declares itself only in the file it lives in is a stub nobody counts**, and it is precisely the failure mode the phase prompt says this document exists to prevent.

 **Fixed rather than described.** It is a fourth entry in `STUBS`, a fourth row in the spec's table and in the back end's README, and the test now asserts four **plus two more**: that every module named in `STUBS` exists on disk, and that **the module which calls itself a stub in prose is in the array.** The second is the negative control on the whole list.

 **What is not real about it, precisely:** a PDF or a `.docx` yields one marker line, **so the receipt strip runs over a marker rather than over the document.** A text-bearing upload IS read and IS stripped. It is honest, it was always honest, and it was invisible.

Both numbers are right and the note works it through.** Fourteen were archived by the fold phases — Phase 104 four, Phase 107 three, Phase 108 seven. **The fifteenth is the retired Client Journey (FINAL)**: superseded on 3 September, found to exist on disk nowhere, and recovered by Phase 100 on 8 September from an attachment on the developer handover pack. **No fold phase could have archived it, because it was already retired.** "Fifteen" and "the fold archived fourteen" are both true and neither should be corrected into the other.

### The harness had to be told, and it is a deliberate change with a reason

 **Suite M4 asserts every document in the developer handover pack is on disk, and the Developer Brief is one of them.** Archiving it would have failed M4. **The entry was repointed at the archived path and a new entry added for the spec that replaced it** — the same pattern Phase 104 used for the journey wireframe, and for the same reason: the pack still requires the file, because it is the only record of the brief as written. **The reads are by NAME, not by index**, which is not a stylistic choice — when Phase 104 archived the wireframe, `HANDOVER[5]` silently became a different document and M5 started failing against a file that was never the handler.

 **Six new assertions, suite M4a**, and one of them is the interesting one: **every module named in the code's own ****`STUBS`**** array must appear in the spec's stub table.** A spec listing fewer stubs than the code is a shorter list a reader would trust. A companion assertion checks `STUBS` is non-empty, so the check cannot pass vacuously.

### THE NODE DECISION PARTIALLY REVERSES THE 1 SEPTEMBER WORDPRESS DECISION, AND HERE IS WHY

 **Recorded because the phase prompt required it recorded rather than assumed.** On **1 September 2026** Lakhbir answered the platform question with the larger of the two readings: _"wordpress is the whole back end and front end."_ That is PHP, MySQL, WP-Cron, WordPress users and roles, everything in one — and it means everything already built is **rebuilt, wrapped or dropped, not connected.**

 **On 6 September the build was scoped in Node and TypeScript**, and the seven phases were built that way. **The reversal is narrow and it was taken on one fact:** the engine, the eleven data modules, the upload handler and every assertion in the suites already are TypeScript, and **a PHP port of a tax engine that must keep 640 assertions green is the largest and riskiest job in the project.** Porting it first, before anything had ever run, would have meant re-proving every tax position in a second language before a single screen existed.

 **The fallback is defined and nothing is thrown away either way.** If the host can run a Node process, this ships behind WordPress and the integration is a reverse proxy and a shared session story. **If it cannot, this becomes the executable specification the PHP rebuild is tested against** — the tests define _done_ in both worlds, and 1,563 passing assertions describing the behaviour precisely are worth more to a PHP rebuild than a prose specification would have been.

 **WHAT MAKES IT ONLY PARTIAL, AND WHY IT IS NOT CLOSED.** _Whether the host can run Node has never been answered._ The question went to the host on 3 September along with the backup-exclusion question, and the reply — _"Yes and yes"_ — reads equally as _I will send them_ and as _the host said yes to both_. **That ambiguity is itself an open question in CAPREBATE QUESTIONS**, under the title _"Did you send the two hosting questions, or were 'yes and yes' the host's answers?"_, and until it is resolved **the reversal is a working assumption with a stated fallback, not a decision.** The Developer Spec says so in §5.3 and names it as the question that most changes the price.

# PHASE 110 — 9 September 2026. The postcode table got somewhere to live, LEG-E4 got an input, and a stale table finally does something

 **Board item 12993800139, plus 13004035199 as a fourth job carried in from Phase 107a. Model: Opus. Run on the Mac.**

 **What it inherited.** A finished, proven resolver that nothing called. Built 8 September and run end to end against the real 2,729,091-line ONS download — 2,657,599 postcodes, 352 billing authorities, 0 malformed. It had no home for its 292 MB output, nobody to refresh it, and no consumer.

## Job 1 — where a 292 MB table lives, costed by running it rather than reasoning about it

 **The phase prompt offered three options and warned against defaulting to the easiest. It also mis-stated the cost of that easiest one, which is the finding.** `caprebate-postcode-store-costing.cjs` was written to measure all three on synthetic data at the real shape and scale, in separate processes so a resident-set figure measures the option rather than the run.

|   |  (a) JSON in memory |  (b) SQLite, read-only |  (c) trimmed to England and Wales |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  File on disk |  290.3 MB |  **74.5 MB** |  267.1 MB |
|  Held in the heap |  310.4 MB |  — |  296.8 MB |
|  Process resident set |  630.9 MB |  **~11 MB over baseline** |  618 MB |
|  One lookup |  0.51 µs |  7.55 µs |  0.51 µs |
|  Rows kept |  all |  all |  2,444,991 of 2,657,599 |

 **The prompt costed option (a) at "~292 MB resident per process". That is the FILE size.** The process sits at about 630 MB, and the ingest that builds the file needs a 10 GB heap. On a small server that option does not make things simple — it decides how much memory the whole application must be given, per process, forever.

 **Option (c) was measured and does not work.** Dropping Scotland removes 8% of the rows and **4% of the heap**, leaving option (a) at 297 MB against option (b)'s 11 MB. Trimming is a rounding error on a storage strategy, not one.

 **Built: (b), as a SEPARATE read-only file rather than a table in the application database.** The back end already runs node:sqlite so putting it there is nearly free — and wrong. This is public reference data rebuilt in full every quarter from a free download; inside the application database every backup and restore carries 75 MB nobody would miss, and a quarterly refresh becomes a migration against live client records instead of a file swap. Most of the disk saving is not SQLite being clever: it is that 2.66 million copies of 352 authority names become 352 rows.

 **Both adapters ship behind a ****`PostcodeStore`**** port**, and the resolver now takes a source rather than a table. **K3 asserts the resolver behaves identically over either adapter, including how it FAILS** — that matching is the acceptance test for the port.

 **And the part of (c) that was kept.** Its correctness point was real: a Scottish postcode must refuse as OUTSIDE THE SERVED JURISDICTION, not as "not in table". That refusal was built — in the resolver, driven by a served set **passed in from ****`CB_JURIS.SERVED`**** and restated nowhere**. Trimming would have made our coverage a property of a data file: flipping that one boolean to add Scotland would then have silently required a re-ingest, and until somebody ran one every Scottish client would be refused by a table that no longer meant to refuse them.

## Job 2 — wired to LEG-E4, and LEG-E4 is still off

 **`leg_e4_location_and_contract_size`**** ships false and stays false**, and the factor table it would need is still empty, so even a gate flipped by hand could not produce a figure from a price book nobody has bought. Both asserted.

 **The chain still stops at the purchase.** `E_LOCATION_KEY_TABLE_NOT_LOADED` and its message naming which half is solved were already built and tested, and are **called, not re-implemented**.

 **The one thing a wiring change could break.** With the gate off, LEG-E4 returns 1.0 with `applied: false`. With the gate on and no key it must refuse. A wiring layer is exactly where those get confused — catch the refusal, hand the cost model no key, and a gate-on run quietly produces the gate-off answer: a 1.0 nobody chose, in a claim.

 **So the wiring never decides which of the two it is in.** It asks the cost model's own `gateOn`, which was exported for this so the `opts.gates` override every test uses is honoured — a second copy of a three-line rule is still a second copy. Gate off, it returns that function's own object unmodified and resolves no postcode at all. Gate on, every failure is rethrown and there is no `try` anywhere below it.

 **Proved by breaking it, not by reading it.** Three deliberate mutations, each caught: wrapping the resolution in a `try` that falls back — **3 failures**; disabling the jurisdiction check — **1**; making an expired table serve instead of refuse — **1**. Restored to 23 / 0.

## Job 3 — what a stale table does, and who refreshes it

 **`tableIsStale()`**** had existed since 8 September and nothing read it.** A staleness report nobody consumes is a comment with a return type.

 **Two thresholds, because two different things go wrong as the table ages and only one is dangerous.** New postcodes go missing — already refused loudly and correctly, and age makes that more common rather than wrong. But **a reorganised council resolves to its old name**, silently, into a surveyor's report; reorganisations take effect each 1 April. So: under 120 days, normal. **120 days to a year, the answer is still given and carries ****`ONS_TABLE_STALE`** in the same `flags` array the terminated-postcode flag uses, so it travels with the answer exactly as the licence attribution does. **Over a year, it refuses** — a table that old has been through an April, and a year is long enough that nobody can present the refresh as an oversight. **Never-ingested is not stale** and says so in different words, because it is a different job for a different person.

 **And the duty is written down**, in `00-START-HERE/Caprebate-ONS-Postcode-Table-Refresh-Procedure-v1.md`: who, when, the exact command, what happens if nobody does it, and a log whose first row is the real run of 8 September. **A quarterly duty that lives only in a code comment is a duty nobody performs.**

 **The column-name check is in it twice.** ONS renames the local-authority column every release — `laua`, `LAD25CD`, `lad26cd` — and the ingest falls back to a pattern rather than failing, which is right and is exactly why a person has to read the line it prints. The region column added by this phase gets the same treatment and the same instruction.

## Job 4, carried in from Phase 107a — the region, which never needed the price book

 **Board item 13004035199.** Every surveyor rate library entry was keyed on the constant `REGION_NOT_CAPTURED`, so a surveyor's own figures were proposed back to them across the whole country.

 **The finding: this was recorded as waiting on a £330 purchase and the purchase was never what stood in the way.** The price book supplies the FACTORS. Which council sits in which region is **Office for National Statistics geography, published free under the Open Government Licence, and NSPL carries it on every postcode row**. That is the same shape of mistake as the one this module found about LEG-E4 itself.

 **Only the thirteen region NAMES were taken from the book — a vocabulary, so this project has one regional grouping rather than three.** Not one factor entered the repository, and **R1 asserts that mechanically**: a decimal appearing anywhere in the region vocabulary fails the test. The three price-book PDFs remain under the provenance quarantine the 6 September surveyor note recorded.

 **Eleven of the thirteen map with no judgement at all. London refuses.** The book prices Inner London at 1.05 and Outer at 1.00 — about 5% on a whole cost plan — without saying which boroughs are which, and there are two published definitions differing by two boroughs. **Outer London is the cheaper of the two, so a silent default would have been the answer that suits us.** The question is now in front of the surveyor.

 **The constant is still what a surveyor sees today**, because no deployment has a postcode table installed. What changed is that the screen now names **which** of the four things is missing instead of printing `region-not-captured` and leaving them to guess.

## Two live defects found on the way, neither of them in scope

 **The ingest runner crashed on its own usage message.** It printed `NSPL_COLUMNS_ASSUMED` without importing it, so running it with no arguments died with a `ReferenceError` instead of telling the operator what to do — on the exact path an operator hits first. Fixed and re-run.

 **`--out`**** had a default**, so a run that wanted only the SQLite file also wrote 290 MB of JSON nobody asked for. It now requires at least one named output.

## Proven end to end, on a file rather than in a unit test

 **A six-row NSPL file of the real shape was ingested to a real SQLite database and resolved through the whole chain.** Cardiff → Wales. Manchester → North West. Westminster → refused as the open London question. Edinburgh → refused as outside our coverage. Belfast → refused on the licence, before the table was read. A terminated postcode → refused as terminated. The LEG-E4 seam returned 1.0 / `applied: false` with the gate off and **refused at the purchase link with the gate forced on**. Not the 2.7 million-row file — that was 8 September, and this run tested the wiring rather than the data.

## PHASE 111 — 9 September 2026 — Finish the brand rename, and write down the rule for what must never be renamed

 **Model: Opus. Machine: Lakhbir's Mac.** The rename to Caprebate had been declared complete twice and was not. This phase closed it and — more usefully — recorded the convention, because a decision nobody wrote down is what took this to a third phase.

### THE COUNT, RE-DERIVED — and the prompt was wrong twice

 One query over the board (339 items, 303 assets), tallied in code:

|   |  Before |  After |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  Attachment filenames carrying a dead brand |  **38** |  **1**, kept on purpose |
|  Board item names carrying a dead brand |  **27** |  **3**, kept on purpose |

 **The prompt said 39 and it is 38** — the thirty-ninth, the full specification, is already clean on its item. **The prompt said six HTML artefacts and there are five**, for the same reason. Two earlier prompts had quoted five and nine. Re-derive; never inherit.

### THE RULE — this is the part worth keeping

 **An entity reference is renamed. A citation is not.** A citation is a file path, a verbatim quotation, a code identifier, or a dated statement about a named thing where the name _is_ the fact. Renaming a citation does not update the record, it falsifies it. Phase 100 established this on the ASA/CAP audit; Phase 111 applied it across the board and wrote it into `README-file-index.md` under _Phase 111 — the brand rename finished, and what was deliberately left_.

 **And the corollary that stopped one wrong preservation.** Item _VERIFY: were BUILDING_REGS_COMPLETION and GRANT_FUNDING_AGREEMENT actually built…_ cited `phase3/ledgerstone-document-pipeline.ts` — **a path that has not existed since Phase 78 renamed the file**. That citation was corrected, not preserved. **A citation is only evidence while it points at something.**

### WHAT WAS KEPT, AND WHY

-  **`ledgerstone-site.html`** on the LEG-E1 engine-remediation item. Byte-identical to the legacy site fork of 19 June 2026 at the Development root — **not the engine**, which is `Caprebate site.html`. The _E-1/E-2 PROPAGATION_ item cites that exact filename with a measured count of 47 unremediated hits taken against it.

-  **Three item names**: _E-1/E-2 PROPAGATION_ (cites the path plus the count); _PHASE 69 — DONE… six governance docs still say Ledgerstone_ (a dated finding); _RENAME EVERYTHING TO CAPREBATE_ (the rename item, recording the pre-rename state). -  **Three document bodies**, each of which now ends with a **Brand-rename note** listing exactly what was left: one `ledgerstone-site.html` path, two `ledgerstone-full-specification-v8.html` paths, and decision row **D7** — _"keep the name Health Capital, restructure for Ledgerstone"_ — whose two names are the point of the sentence.

## PHASE 112 — The pricing arithmetic rebuilt on the base that was actually decided (9 September 2026)

 **Five documents priced jobs on ****5% of lifetime relief****. Q55 settled the fee on 3 September 2026 as ****5% of the capital allowances identified****. Phase 101 banned quotation from all five on 8 September; this phase made the numbers true and removed every banner.** The decided base is 1/(tax rate) larger — 2.5× at 40%, 4× at 25% — and, more importantly, **it does not contain the claimant's tax rate at all**, so every conclusion resting on claimant type had to be re-derived rather than re-worded.

### The finding, and it is a reversal rather than a correction

 **The central conclusion of both minimum-fee papers does not survive.** They concluded that _"the minimum is not a floor, it is the price"_ because 5% of lifetime relief did not overtake a £5,000 minimum until a dental purchase of £1.1m — £1.8m if company-held. **On the decided base it overtakes at £444,444, and there is one crossover per sector instead of two.**

|  Sector |  Minimum |  Crossover now |  Was, unincorporated |  Was, company |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  Dental / GP |  £5,000 |  **£444,444** |  £1,111,111 |  £1,777,778 |
|  Care home |  £7,500 |  **£500,000** |  £1,250,000 |  £2,000,000 |
|  Private hospital |  £7,500 |  **£428,571** |  £1,071,429 |  £1,714,286 |

 **On the business plan's own assumed mix the minimum binds on NONE of the four sectors and 0% of jobs by volume**, where the plan said three of four and 90%. The launch-minimum recommendation was restated rather than quietly kept: the minimum is now a floor for the small end, and the pricing page must lead with the percentage and name its base in the same sentence.

 **Three further reversals fell out of it, and each is recorded in the document it belongs to.** The break-even spread collapsed from 2.2× to **1.35×** (£319,111 to £429,333 at a hundred jobs a year), which means **a minimum job size is no longer arithmetically wrong** — the 1 September decision stands, but on the channel and good-work grounds, not on the numbers, and both papers now say so. The rate card's argument that the cost base supports only a 5–15% portfolio discount is **withdrawn**: the six-care-home example now makes £18,050 a home against £6,250 of cost, so a 40% discount would still leave £16,200. And the business plan's headline moved from **−£4,425 with a £147,000 funding requirement** to **+£1,193,700, break-even in month 10, and a £77,976 trough**.

 **One figure moved the wrong way and it is the one to watch.** Our fee is 5% of allowances, which is **12.5% of an unincorporated client's lifetime relief and 20.0% of a company's**, on every job at every size — and **89% to 333% of what they relieve in their first year.** On the superseded base it was 5% of their relief by construction. That is now stated in terms in four of the five documents and flagged to the accountant register.

### The two readings, priced rather than resolved

 **Whether the £5,000 / £7,500 launch minimum FEE survived Lakhbir's 1 September decision that there is no minimum JOB SIZE was left open on purpose.** Both readings are priced throughout. **They price the assumed book identically** (£18,325 a job either way, because the minimum binds on nothing in it) and differ only below each sector's crossover — a £300,000 dental job is £5,000 under one reading and £3,375 under the other, and pays at a hundred jobs a year under the first but not the second. **So it is a decision about the smallest jobs and about self-description, not about revenue.**

### What was built, and why nothing was computed by hand

 **No calculator was invented.** `04-phase-work/phase9/caprebate-job-economics.cjs` gained a Section 9 — `claimantTypeEntersTheFee`, `feeOnAllowances`, `allowancesFromPurchasePrice`, `bandedFee`, `rescaledBands`, `crossoverPurchasePrice`, `priceJobBothReadings`, `blendedFeePerJob`, `effectiveRateOnLifetimeRelief` — all with the fee rate, sector yield and candidate minimum **injected**, never held. **Suite G, 17 tests, asserts every replacement figure**, reads the 5% out of the shipped engine, and **reproduces the papers' published OLD-basis crossovers to the pound before replacing them**, so the model can be seen to describe the thing it supersedes. Proved it can fail: reintroducing the tax-rate multiplier on purpose turned 8 tests red.

 **`03-app/caprebate-business-plan-model.cjs`**** was rebased in the same pass**, so the 24-month forecast, ramp, cash-lag and sensitivity figures are produced by running it rather than by scaling the old ones. `feeOptionA` and `feeOptionB` were kept unchanged — deleting a resolved fork makes the resolution unreadable. **Its cost side was not touched**, and Suite B still asserts it cell-for-cell against the module.

### What ran, at the close

```text

node 03-app/caprebate-regression.cjs --package      640 pass / 0 fail / 4 xfail
cd 04-phase-work/phase3 && node --test              385 pass / 0 fail
cd 04-phase-work/phase9 && node --test              314 pass / 0 fail   (was 297)
node 03-app/caprebate-figure-drift.cjs              0 present-tense failures - GREEN
node 09-app/engine/tools/verify-extraction.cjs      21 checks, 0 failures
node 09-app/engine/tools/extract.cjs --check        exit 0 after regenerating
```

 **1,339 passing assertions across the three harnesses**, and the drift checker earned its keep: it went red on the phase9 count the moment Suite G landed, and named the three documents asserting 297 in the present tense.

### Two things worth knowing for next time

 **The extraction manifest hashes the WHOLE site file, not the engine slice.** Correcting two sentences of HTML copy in `Caprebate site.html` marked the package stale even though `verify-extraction` passed all 21 byte-for-byte checks. Re-running `extract.cjs` changed exactly one file, `manifest.json`. **`--check`**** does exit 1 when stale** — an earlier reading that it exited 0 was measuring `tail`, not `node`.

 **A file's character count is not its byte count.** The presigned upload declares a size; one of the five was declared 326 bytes short because the edit script printed `len(str)` and the file is UTF-8 full of £ and —. **The upload succeeded and the downloaded object was byte-identical to disk**, so the declared size is metadata, but the counts should come from `wc -c`.

## PHASE 113 — The drift trap that could not see the package, and a possessive that outlived the rename (9 September 2026)

 **Two things Phase 102 found while extracting the engine and deliberately did not fix**, because its acceptance test was that the harness reports the same totals before and after, and touching an assertion or a client-facing string there would have destroyed that comparison. **Both were re-derived here before anything was changed, and both were still open.** Run from the Mac copy of the tree (`OneDrive - Aqlios LTD/.../Development/Caprebate`), which is the copy this machine can reach.

### Job 1 — Suite Q's yield-band drift trap was blind in package mode

 Suite Q's Q2 exists to catch two copies of one constant diverging: every sector engine carries its own `YIELD_BAND` and the funnel sizes the client's only number from `CB_BAND`, so Q2 asserts they are still identical. **It built its ****`declared`**** side by running a regular expression over ****`src`**** — and ****`src`**** is the SITE file in BOTH modes.** So `--package` compared the _site's_ sector bands against the _package's_ shared table, and a band that diverged in the package's own sector files passed unnoticed.

 **Reproduced before the fix rather than inherited from the prompt.** Moving the care_homes purchase band to `[0.20,0.55]` in `09-app/engine/src/generated/sector-care_homes.js` left package mode **green at 640**; only `verify-extraction.cjs` caught it, failing 1 of its 21 byte checks. Phase 102 saw the same thing at 634. The prompt's claim was exact.

 **The fix is one expression and no new assertion**, as instructed. `declared` is now built from the loaded `ENGINES[sector].YIELD_BAND` — the lifted engines expose it and so does every package module — and **the key is taken from the engine's own declaration rather than from the ****`SECTORS`**** list**, so an engine that declared its band under the wrong sector name is still caught by the key check instead of being silently renamed into agreement. Both regexes are gone. One check was renamed from _"all five sector engines were found in the source"_ to _"…declared a band, and under their own name"_, because it no longer reads the source; a check name is not an assertion and the count did not move.

 **Proved able to fail in both directions, which is the entire point of the change:**

```text
package band diverged   package mode  639 pass / 1 fail   Q2 FAILS   (before this phase: 640 / 0 — blind)
                        site mode     640 pass / 0 fail   correct: the site really is untouched
site band diverged      site mode     639 pass / 1 fail   Q2 FAILS   (unchanged behaviour)
```

 **Same suite, same two checks, same totals in both modes** — so the before/after comparison the extraction rests on is still readable, which the prompt made the condition of the work.

### Job 2 — `Caprebate’ own reading`, on the face of every estimate ever produced

 `Caprebate site.html:1123`, inside `CB_PLANT.bandCaveats()`, which all five `runEngine` functions call at the top of their assumptions list. **It survived the whole brand rename, which rewrote the name beside it and left the apostrophe.** Corrected to `Caprebate’s own reading` — one line, one byte, diffed against the backup to confirm nothing else moved. The package was re-cut with `tools/extract.cjs` (`shared.js` and `manifest.json` changed, nothing hand-edited) and `verify-extraction.cjs` returned to 21 / 0.

 **No harness check broke on the corrected text.** Suite Q4 reaches that caveat only through `/assessed, not independently calibrated/i`, which the correction does not touch. Nothing had to be updated to keep a suite green, and nothing was reverted.

### And two more of the same rename artefact, which re-deriving the premise found

 The prompt said _one occurrence_, and that is true of the site file. Searching the whole live tree rather than only the named file found the identical broken possessive in two more places, both one-character fixes, both made here:

|  File |  Text |  What it is |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  `04-phase-work/phase3/caprebate-name-exclusion.ts:313` |  `no connection whatsoever to Caprebate’ client` |  the `note` on the planning-comments source — **the highest-risk entry in the name exclusion register** |
|  `04-phase-work/phase3/caprebate-client-doc-ingestion.ts:193` |  `Caprebate’ server never holds the file` |  a comment on where the ingestion boundary actually is |

 **The register's exported document was already right.** `08-monday-doc-exports/12818313893__Item-7-Name-Exclusion-Register-and-Automated-Assertion.md` says `Caprebate's` at both lines 212 and 631. **The rename fixed the document and missed the source**, so the two had disagreed silently ever since. They agree again. No test asserted either string, and phase3 stayed at 385. **Zero occurrences of the broken possessive now remain anywhere in the live tree** — backups, `_archive/`, `08-monday-doc-exports/` and the dead `ledgerstone all/` lineage excluded on purpose.

# Phase 113a — local time, a client who can move their own call, and the last of a dead column

 **9 September 2026. Board item 13000144499. Three jobs, all three built.** All three were left by Phase 105 and named in its record.

## DONE

 **JOB 1 — local time. BUILT.** The booking system stored, compared _and printed_ everything in UTC. Britain is UTC for about four months a year and an hour ahead for the other eight, so staff setting "09:00 to 17:00" in June were setting ten to six, and a client offered "Wednesday at 09:00" would have arrived at ten. Nobody had reported it because nobody had used it.

 New file `09-app/backend/src/web/localtime.ts` — **the only file in the application that names a timezone**. The offset is asked of `Intl` at the instant in question; nothing anywhere knows that Britain is ever an hour ahead. Storage and comparison are unchanged: every stored moment and every value on the wire is still a `Z`-terminated ISO-8601 string.

 **THE HARD HALF WAS THE WORKING TIMES, AND THE ANSWER IS WRITTEN INTO THE FILE.** `working_times` holds minutes from midnight against a weekday with no date, so "09:00" has no single UTC answer across a year. **They are LOCAL minutes against a LOCAL weekday**, converted per candidate day where slots are generated, because a person's hours are local hours and a UTC reading would move everybody's week by an hour twice a year. `schedule.ts` decision 3 is the long-form reasoning; `isBookable` is the exact mirror.

 **Both awkward mornings are handled rather than rounded away.** `instantsForLocalMinute` returns **zero** instants for a local time in the March gap, **two** for one in the October overlap, one the rest of the year — so no slot is offered at a time that does not happen, and both of the October 01:30s are offerable because they are two real moments.

 **`startOfDay`****, ****`startOfWeek`**** and ****`addDays`**** were renamed** to `startOfLocalDay`, `startOfLocalWeek`, `addLocalDays`, and the rename is the point: a "day" that began at `00:00Z` put the first hour of every summer day in the previous column. A local day is 23, 24 or 25 hours long and a test says which is which.

 `test/localtime.test.ts`, **15 tests**, everything asserted twice on real dates either side of both 2026 transitions — 29 March and 25 October. **Proved able to fail:** with the offset hard-coded to 60, nine of fifteen fail; hard-coded to 0, the same nine fail. There is no constant that passes.

 **JOB 2 — a client can move their own call. BUILT.** `POST /portal/bookings/{id}`. Times from `publicSlots` (the funnel-close picker's own function, people taken out); the write through `isBookable` at the moment of writing with `ignoreBooking` set; the move into `booking_changes` with the client named. **The staff booking page's existing history shows the client's move without a line of new code**, which is the evidence this is the existing mechanism and not a second one.

 **The authorisation is a NEW ROW: ****`booking.move_own`****, CLIENT only, ****`ownBusiness`****.** Deliberately not `CLIENT` added to `booking.write` — that action means _own and arrange a client call_, it builds the diary through `bookableUserIds`, and it gates the whole back-office calendar section. A test asserts a client is still refused it, and adding `CLIENT` to that row fails the suite.

 **The two decisions, made and stated.** **Two hours' notice, applied at both ends** — a client may not move a call inside two hours of it, nor into the next two hours, because otherwise the rule buys nobody any notice and only changes which call is imminent. **No self-service cancellation, and that is the decision rather than an omission** — a cancel with no replacement time is a lead going cold. What they get is _release_: the slot returns to the pool, the booking row, its channel and its entry point survive with `starts_at` NULL, and the call reappears in the back office's "asked for a time and has not got one" list. **The alternatives are drawn above the way out**, so "none of these work" is reached after looking. `test/portal-booking.test.ts`, **17 tests**; the notice window set to zero fails four of them.

 **JOB 3 — ****`businesses.preferred_contact`**** is GONE. THE REBUILD CAME OUT CLEAN, SO IT WAS KEPT.** `migrations/007-retire-preferred-contact.sql`, the twelve-step SQLite procedure. Migration 004 had ended the column and could not delete it — SQLite refuses `DROP COLUMN` on a column named in a table CHECK — and declined the rebuild because **thirteen tables carry a foreign key into ****`businesses`**.

 **`PRAGMA foreign_key_check`**** returns rows; it does not abort**, and a migration runner executing a file has nothing to branch on. It is turned into a _failure_ by a one-column guard table whose CHECK demands zero, fed the count of violations: any violation aborts the migration and it is never recorded as applied. **Proved able to fail** against a deliberately broken database before it was kept. The two retirement triggers went with the table on purpose — a trigger naming a column that does not exist is a fossil, not a control — and the dead fallback in `contactFor`, reading a guaranteed NULL since 4 September, went with them.

 **Also done, because a phase that leaves the paperwork has not finished.** The developer register was corrected — it listed _timezone handling_ among eight things a developer must price as new build, and that line went stale within hours of being written. The Developer Spec gained `C6a`, closed `W7`, and had four "every time is UTC" claims corrected. `README-file-index.md` and the back end's own README carry the whole of it. A question went into CAPREBATE QUESTIONS under Lakhbir recording both business decisions — marked as already built to our recommendation, because nothing is waiting on him.

## What was found that the prompt did not know

 **THE PROMPT SAID THE PLACES THAT PRINT A TIME ARE "FEW AND ARE ALL IN ONE FILE". THEY WERE NOT.** It named four functions across three files. There were also raw ISO slices on the engaged-client page, a hand-built subject line in the calendar invitation — **addressed to a client**, and reading "09:00 UTC" for a call at ten — the receipt-contract trace on the client's own document page, and the calendar's day headings. A prompt is a claim, not a fact.

 **TWO PUBLISHED FIGURES WERE ALREADY STALE ON THE DAY THEY WERE WRITTEN.** The Developer Spec's own "run these" block said `phase9` was **245** (it was 314) and the back end **293** (it was 310 before this phase). Both corrected. **Neither was caught by the drift checker**, and the reason is a real gap: the back end is not one of its three derived truths, and a figure inside a fenced _run this, see this_ block carries no prose marker so it lands in the bucket that never fails. That is now **Phase 113e**.

## NOT DONE

 **The drift checker watches three harnesses and the back end is not one of them; and a figure on a command line is treated as prose — BUILDABLE — new Phase 113e, written and inserted before the sweep.**

 **The Browser pane returned a blank frame when asked to screenshot the portal — NOT A DEFECT IN THIS WORK AND NOT ROUTED ANYWHERE.** The page's own DOM and computed layout were correct and were read directly, and the whole flow was driven end to end over HTTP against the demo server. It is recorded here only so that nobody reads "verified" as "looked at a picture of it".

 **Nothing else. Every one of the three jobs is built, and the phase claimed no ground it did not take.**

 **Correction to the two figures above, made in the same session and before this record was left.** The back end closed at **343**, not 342, and the client-move suite at **eighteen** tests, not seventeen. The eighteenth was written after the first run: `tooLateToMove` is arithmetic, and every moment in the past is less than two hours away — so a client whose call was yesterday was being told it was _"less than 2 hours away"_. The rule was right and the sentence was not. There are now two sentences and a test that a call which has already passed is described as one. **33 new assertions, not 32.**
